topics.BLS: Basic life support & chain of survival
topics.MI: Acute coronary syndrome / MI in primary care

cards.q: What is basic life support (BLS)?
cards.a:
• Care given by **first responders, healthcare providers and public-safety staff**
• To anyone with **cardiac arrest, respiratory distress or an obstructed airway**
• Aim: keep oxygenated blood flowing to brain and heart until advanced care arrives
cards.m: BLS buys time - it is the bridge to the defibrillator and ALS team.

cards.q: What components does basic life support include?
cards.a:
• **A**irway
• **B**reathing
• **C**irculation (chest compressions)
• **AED** - automated external defibrillation
• Management of **choking / foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO)**
Note: slides write 'BSL'; the correct abbreviation is **BLS**.
cards.m: ABC + D (defib) + choking.

cards.q: What is the chain of survival, and what are its links for adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
cards.a:
• A **sequence of critical, time-sensitive actions** that maximises survival from cardiac arrest
• Links (AHA adult OHCA): **early recognition + call for help (MERS 999)** → **early high-quality CPR** → **rapid defibrillation** → advanced resuscitation → post-cardiac arrest care → recovery
• Every minute without CPR/defibrillation reduces survival by roughly **7-10%**
cards.m: Call - Compress - Shock - Advanced - After-care - Recovery.

cards.q: What is the order of the BLS steps taught for primary care?
cards.a:
• **D**anger
• **R**esponse
• **S**hout for help
• **A**irway
• **B**reathing (with pulse check)
• **C**irculation - chest compressions
• **D**efibrillation (AED)
• Reassessment every 2 min / 5 cycles
cards.m: DRS ABCD - 'Doctors ABCD'.

cards.q: What does the 'Danger' step of BLS involve?
cards.a:
• Make sure **you, the victim and bystanders are safe**
• Wear **PPE** - gloves, apron, mask
• Look for hazards: **blood spills, sharps, electric wires, unsteady beds or trolleys**
• Never become a second casualty
cards.m: A dead rescuer saves no one.

cards.q: How do you check for a response, and what do you do if the victim responds?
cards.a:
• **Gently tap the shoulders** and ask loudly ‘Are you OK?’
• If he **responds**: leave him in the position found, get help if needed, **re-assess regularly**
• If **no response**: shout for help and proceed to airway
cards.m: Tap and talk.

cards.q: How does 'shout for help' differ for in-hospital (IHCA) vs out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)?
cards.a:
• **IHCA** (e.g. in the clinic): shout ‘Emergency! Emergency! Bring the **resuscitation trolley and defibrillator**!’ and activate **Code Blue** if available
• **OHCA**: send someone to **fetch an AED**
• A **lone responder with a mobile phone** dials **MERS 999** (speaker on) and **starts CPR**
cards.m: Inside: trolley + Code Blue. Outside: AED + 999.

cards.q: How is the head tilt-chin lift performed?
cards.a:
• Place one hand on the **forehead** and gently **tilt the head back**
• Fingertips **under the bony point of the chin** - lift the chin
• Opens the airway by lifting the **tongue off the posterior pharynx**
• Avoid pressing on the soft tissue under the chin
cards.m: The tongue is the commonest airway obstruction in the unconscious.

cards.q: How is the jaw thrust performed, and when is it preferred over head tilt-chin lift?
cards.a:
• **Index and middle fingers** push the **posterior angles of the mandible upwards**; thumbs push down on the cheeks to open the mouth
• Preferred when **cervical spine injury is suspected** (trauma, fall, diving) - opens the airway **without extending the neck**
• If jaw thrust fails, airway takes priority - use head tilt
cards.m: Trauma? Thrust the jaw, spare the neck.

cards.q: How long should a healthcare worker spend checking breathing and pulse?
cards.a:
• **Not more than 10 seconds**
• Look at **chest, neck and face** for breathing while **simultaneously feeling the carotid pulse**
• If unsure whether a pulse is present - **start compressions**
cards.m: Ten seconds, then compress.

cards.q: What is agonal breathing, and how should you act on it?
cards.a:
• Slow, irregular **gasps** seen in the first minutes after cardiac arrest
• It is **not normal breathing**
• No breathing / agonal breathing **+ no pulse** = cardiac arrest → **start chest compressions** immediately
cards.m: Gasping is not breathing - it is a sign of arrest.

cards.q: A victim has a definite pulse but no or abnormal breathing. What do you do?
cards.a:
• **Respiratory arrest** - give **rescue breaths only**
• **1 breath every 6 seconds = 10 breaths/min** (adult)
• Re-check the pulse about every **2 minutes**; start compressions if it is lost
cards.m: Pulse present: 1 breath every 6 s.

cards.q: Where and how should the hands be placed for adult chest compressions?
cards.a:
• **Heel of one hand** in the **centre of the chest, lower half of the sternum**
• Other hand on top, **fingers interlocked** - no pressure on the ribs
• **Arms straight**, shoulders **vertically above** the chest
• Patient on a **firm surface**
cards.m: Straight arms, shoulders over hands - use body weight, not biceps.

cards.q: What rate and depth define high-quality adult chest compressions?
cards.a:
• Rate: **100-120 compressions/min**
• Depth: **at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm**
• Allow **complete recoil** after each compression
• **Minimise interruptions**
cards.m: Push hard (5-6 cm), push fast (100-120) - the tempo of ‘Stayin’ Alive’.

cards.q: Why must the chest be allowed to recoil completely between compressions?
cards.a:
• Recoil creates **negative intrathoracic pressure** → **venous return** refills the heart
• Leaning on the chest lowers **cardiac output and coronary perfusion pressure**
• So the next compression has blood to eject
cards.m: Compression empties the pump; recoil refills it.

cards.q: What is the adult compression-to-ventilation ratio, and how should each breath be given?
cards.a:
• **30 compressions : 2 breaths**
• Each breath delivered **over 1 second**
• Give just enough volume for **visible chest rise**
cards.m: 30:2, one-second breaths, watch the chest rise.

cards.q: Why should hyperventilation be avoided during CPR?
cards.a:
• Raises **intrathoracic pressure** → reduces **venous return and cardiac output**
• Lowers **coronary and cerebral perfusion**
• Causes **gastric inflation** → regurgitation and aspiration
• So: 1-second breaths, only enough to see chest rise
cards.m: More air is not more life.

cards.q: How often should the person doing chest compressions be changed, and why?
cards.a:
• Switch compressor every **5 cycles or 2 minutes**
• **Fatigue** quickly reduces depth and rate, often unnoticed by the rescuer
• Swap during the rhythm/pulse check to keep the pause short
cards.m: Two minutes, swap hands.

cards.q: How long may chest compressions be interrupted during CPR?
cards.a:
• Keep pauses to **less than 10 seconds** (for breaths, rhythm analysis, shock)
• Aim for chest compressions during **more than 60% (ideally >80%)** of resuscitation time
• Every pause lets coronary perfusion pressure fall, and it takes several compressions to rebuild
cards.m: No flow when you stop - keep pauses under 10 s.

cards.q: How is bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation performed using the E-C clamp?
cards.a:
• Rescuer **directly above the victim’s head**
• Mask positioned using the **bridge of the nose** as guide
• **C**: thumb + index finger press mask edges onto the face
• **E**: remaining 3 fingers lift the **angle of the jaw**; head tilt
• Squeeze bag over **1 second**, watch for chest rise
cards.m: C seals the mask, E lifts the jaw.

cards.q: Mouth-to-mask vs bag-valve-mask ventilation: where does the rescuer position themselves?
cards.a:
• **Mouth-to-mask**: rescuer at the **victim’s side** (single rescuer can alternate compressions and breaths)
• **BVM**: rescuer **directly above the head** (best with 2 rescuers)
• Both: tight seal, head tilt-chin lift, breath over **1 second**, avoid hyperventilation
cards.m: Mask alone - by the side. Bag - at the head.

cards.q: Where are AED pads placed on an adult?
cards.a:
• Switch on AED (or defibrillator in AED mode); pads on **bare chest**
• Pad 1: **right upper chest, below the clavicle**
• Pad 2: **cardiac apex** (left mid-axillary line)
• Then follow the **voice/visual prompts**
cards.m: Right under the collarbone, left over the apex - the current crosses the heart.

cards.q: What are the safety steps when an AED advises a shock, and what happens immediately after?
cards.a:
• Nobody touches the victim while the AED **analyses**
• If shock advised: chant ‘**Everybody clear**’, check, press shock (aim within **5 s**)
• **Immediately restart CPR** (compressions) - do **not** stop to check pulse
• If no shock advised: continue CPR and follow prompts
cards.m: Shock, then straight back on the chest.

cards.q: Which cardiac arrest rhythms are shockable?
cards.a:
• **Shockable**: **ventricular fibrillation (VF)** and **pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT)**
• **Non-shockable**: **asystole** and **pulseless electrical activity (PEA)**
• Non-shockable rhythms: CPR + look for reversible causes (4Hs and 4Ts)
cards.m: V's get volts (VF, VT); A and P get pumping.

cards.q: When is the victim reassessed during CPR, and when may resuscitation stop?
cards.a:
• Check for normal breathing and pulse after every **5 cycles or 2 minutes**
• Do not stop until:
• **Victim recovers** - wakes, moves, opens eyes, breathes normally
• **HCW is exhausted**
• **Assistance arrives** to take over
cards.m: Stop only for: Recovery, Relief, or Rescuer exhaustion.

cards.q: Which patient is placed in the recovery position, and what are the key steps?
cards.a:
• For an **unresponsive patient who is breathing normally**
• Near arm at right angles, elbow bent, **palm up**
• Far arm across chest, **back of hand against the near cheek**
• Pull far knee up (foot on ground) and **roll towards you**
• Upper hip and knee at **right angles**; **tilt head back** to keep airway open
• **Check breathing regularly**; be ready to restart CPR
cards.m: Breathing but unconscious → on the side, so the tongue and vomit fall forward.

cards.q: How does paediatric BLS differ from adult BLS?
cards.a:
• **5 initial rescue breaths** before compressions (ERC; asphyxial arrests are commoner)
• Ratio **15:2** with two healthcare rescuers (30:2 if lone rescuer)
• Depth **one-third of chest AP diameter**: about **4 cm infant**, **5 cm child**
• Infant: **two-finger** or **two-thumb encircling** technique; child: one or two hands
• Rate still **100-120/min**
cards.m: Kids arrest from lack of air - so give breaths first and more often.

cards.q: What extra manoeuvre is needed during CPR on a visibly pregnant woman (fundus at or above the umbilicus)?
cards.a:
• **Manual left uterine displacement** (push the uterus to the left) during compressions
• Relieves **aortocaval compression** by the gravid uterus → improves venous return
• Standard hand position and 30:2; early call for obstetric help (perimortem caesarean if no ROSC by about 4-5 min)
cards.m: Two patients - move the uterus off the vena cava.

cards.q: What should an untrained or unwilling bystander do for an adult in cardiac arrest?
cards.a:
• **Hands-only (compression-only) CPR** at 100-120/min until help or AED arrives
• Follow **dispatcher-assisted CPR** instructions from MERS 999
• Early adult arrests are mostly cardiac - blood is still oxygenated for the first few minutes
cards.m: Call and push - no breaths needed to start.

cards.q: Why should chest compressions be performed on a firm surface?
cards.a:
• A soft mattress **absorbs the compression force** → inadequate depth
• Move the patient to the floor or place a **CPR backboard** under them
• Do not delay CPR for long to achieve this
cards.m: Pushing on a mattress compresses the mattress, not the heart.

cards.q: When should you suspect foreign body airway obstruction (choking)?
cards.a:
• Sudden distress **while eating** (adults) or **playing with small objects** (children)
• **Universal sign of choking**: hands clutching the throat
• Sudden inability to speak, cough or breathe, with cyanosis
cards.m: Hands on the throat while eating = choking until proven otherwise.

cards.q: How do you distinguish mild from severe airway obstruction in a choking adult?
cards.a:
• Ask ‘**Are you choking?**’
• **Mild (effective cough)**: can speak, cough forcefully, breathe → **encourage coughing**
• **Severe (ineffective cough)**: cannot speak, silent or weak cough, stridor, cyanosis, unable to breathe → **back blows then abdominal thrusts**
cards.m: Talking and coughing - leave them coughing. Silent - act now.

cards.q: What is the first action for a conscious choking adult who is coughing effectively?
cards.a:
• **Encourage the patient to keep coughing** - a strong cough is the most effective way to clear the airway
• Do **not** give back blows or thrusts yet
• Stay with them and monitor for the cough becoming **ineffective**
cards.m: Never interrupt a good cough.

cards.q: How are back blows given to a choking adult?
cards.a:
• Indicated when the **cough becomes ineffective**
• Stand to the side and behind, **lean the victim forward**
• Give **up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades** with the **heel of your hand**
• Check after each blow whether the obstruction has cleared
cards.m: Lean forward so the object falls out, not further in.

cards.q: How are abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) performed?
cards.a:
• Given if **5 back blows fail**
• Stand behind, **clenched fist between the umbilicus and the ribcage**
• Grasp the fist with the other hand, pull sharply **inwards and upwards**
• **Up to 5 times**
cards.m: Fist above the navel, below the ribs - in and up.

cards.q: What if the obstruction is not relieved after 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts?
cards.a:
• **Continue alternating 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts**
• Keep going until the object is expelled or the victim **becomes unconscious**
• Call for help / ERS early
cards.m: 5 and 5, repeat until clear or collapse.

cards.q: What do you do when a choking victim becomes unconscious?
cards.a:
• **Support the victim carefully to the ground**
• **Immediately activate the Emergency Response Service (ERS)**
• **Start CPR** beginning with chest compressions (30:2)
• Each time you open the airway for breaths, **look in the mouth** for the object
cards.m: Unconscious choking = cardiac arrest algorithm.

cards.q: When is a finger sweep allowed during management of choking?
cards.a:
• Only if the object is **visible** in the mouth - remove it with a finger sweep
• **Never do a blind finger sweep** - it can push the object deeper or injure the pharynx
• If not seen, **continue CPR**
cards.m: See it - sweep it. Can’t see it - don’t sweep.

cards.q: How is choking managed in an infant under 1 year?
cards.a:
• Hold the infant **face down along your forearm, head lower than chest**
• **5 back blows** between the shoulder blades
• Turn face up: **5 chest thrusts** (two fingers on lower sternum, like compressions but sharper and slower)
• **No abdominal thrusts** - risk of **liver and abdominal organ injury**
• Unconscious → start infant CPR
cards.m: Infants: Back and Chest - never the Belly.

cards.q: Which choking victims should receive chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts?
cards.a:
• **Late pregnancy** - the gravid uterus prevents effective abdominal thrusts and risks injury
• **Obese** victims - rescuer cannot encircle the abdomen
• **Infants** (under 1 year)
• Technique: hands on the **lower half of the sternum**, sharp backward thrusts
cards.m: Pregnant, Plump, or Pint-sized → chest thrusts.

cards.q: Why should every patient who received abdominal thrusts be medically reviewed afterwards?
cards.a:
• Abdominal thrusts can cause **internal injuries** - rupture or laceration of abdominal/thoracic viscera, e.g. **stomach, liver, spleen, diaphragm**
• Retained fragments may cause **persistent cough, wheeze or aspiration pneumonia**
• Review for abdominal pain, tenderness, breathing difficulty
cards.m: A successful Heimlich still earns a doctor’s check.

cards.q: Why are chest compressions, rather than more abdominal thrusts, used once a choking victim is unconscious?
cards.a:
• Chest compressions generate **higher intrathoracic pressure** - they act as thrusts that may expel the object
• They also maintain **circulation** if the victim has arrested from hypoxia
• Before each pair of breaths, **look in the mouth** and remove a visible object
cards.m: Compressions do double duty: clear the airway and pump the blood.

cards.q: What is acute coronary syndrome (ACS)?
cards.a:
• A **clinical spectrum** caused by **imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand and supply**
• Usually due to **reduced supply** - plaque rupture with thrombus in a coronary artery
• Spectrum: **NSTE-ACS** (unstable angina, NSTEMI) and **STEMI**
cards.m: Supply-demand mismatch, mostly a supply problem.

cards.q: How are unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI distinguished?
cards.a:
• **Unstable angina**: ischaemic pain, **troponin normal**, ECG normal or ST depression/T inversion
• **NSTEMI**: **troponin raised**, **no persistent ST elevation**
• **STEMI**: **persistent ST elevation** (or new LBBB) + raised troponin - usually complete occlusion
cards.m: Troponin separates UA from NSTEMI; the ECG separates NSTEMI from STEMI.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for acute coronary syndrome?
cards.a:
• **Modifiable**: **hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyle**
• **Non-modifiable**: **increasing age, male sex, family history of CAD**
cards.m: Modifiable = the KK chronic disease clinic list.

cards.q: What is the typical chest pain of myocardial infarction?
cards.a:
• **Retrosternal** chest discomfort - **pressure, tightness, heaviness, squeezing**
• May **radiate** to arm, shoulder, neck, jaw, back or epigastrium
• May occur **at rest or with exertion**; typically lasts >20 min, not relieved by rest
cards.m: Heavy, central, spreading, lasting.

cards.q: What are the atypical presentations of MI, and in whom are they common?
cards.a:
• **Dyspnoea, diaphoresis, epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, syncope, fatigue**
• Common in **elderly, women, diabetics** (autonomic neuropathy → silent ischaemia) and CKD
• Do an ECG in any such patient with unexplained symptoms
cards.m: Old, female, diabetic - MI may not hurt.

cards.q: What should you look for on examination of a patient with suspected MI?
cards.a:
• General: **distress/restlessness, diaphoresis, reduced consciousness**
• Vitals: **BP, HR, RR, SpO2**
• Respiratory: air entry, **bibasal crackles** (pulmonary oedema)
• CVS: **S3 gallop, raised JVP**, pulses, **carotid bruit**, new murmur
• Examination is often normal - it is done to find **complications**
cards.m: Crackles + S3 + raised JVP = failing left ventricle.

cards.q: Which complications of MI should be actively looked for at presentation?
cards.a:
• **Left ventricular failure** / acute pulmonary oedema
• **Cardiogenic shock**
• **Arrhythmias** (VF/VT, heart block)
• Mechanical: **acute mitral regurgitation** (papillary muscle rupture), **ventricular septal rupture** - new pansystolic murmur
cards.m: Pump, rhythm, and plumbing failures.

cards.q: Within what time must a 12-lead ECG be done in suspected ACS?
cards.a:
• Within **10 minutes of first medical contact**
• Repeat if pain recurs or initial ECG is non-diagnostic (serial ECGs every 15-30 min)
• The ECG decides the pathway: **STEMI vs NSTE-ACS**
cards.m: Ten minutes to the ECG.

cards.q: What ECG changes are sought in suspected ACS?
cards.a:
• **ST elevation**
• **ST depression**
• **T wave changes** (inversion, hyperacute T waves)
• **New left bundle branch block (LBBB)** - treated as STEMI equivalent
cards.m: Up, down, T waves, new LBBB.

cards.q: What are the ECG criteria for STEMI?
cards.a:
• New **ST elevation at the J point in ≥2 contiguous leads**:
• **≥1 mm** in all leads other than V2-V3
• **V2-V3**: ≥2 mm in men ≥40 y, ≥2.5 mm in men <40 y, ≥1.5 mm in women
• Or **new/presumed new LBBB** with ischaemic symptoms
cards.m: Two neighbouring leads, one millimetre (two in V2-V3).

cards.q: Which ECG leads correspond to which myocardial territory and artery?
cards.a:
• **Inferior**: II, III, aVF → usually **right coronary artery**
• **Anterior / anteroseptal**: V1-V4 → **left anterior descending**
• **Lateral**: I, aVL, V5-V6 → **circumflex**
• Posterior: ST depression V1-V3 with tall R waves → check V7-V9
cards.m: Inferior = RCA; anterior = LAD; lateral = Circumflex.

cards.q: What blood investigations are sent in suspected ACS?
cards.a:
• **Troponin** (diagnostic marker of myocardial necrosis)
• **Full blood count** (anaemia, bleeding risk)
• **Renal profile** (K+, renal function before contrast/drugs)
• **Lipid profile, blood glucose** (risk factors)
• Never delay transfer of a STEMI waiting for troponin
cards.m: ECG decides STEMI; troponin decides NSTEMI.

cards.q: Does a normal first troponin exclude myocardial infarction?
cards.a:
• **No** - troponin rises about **3-6 hours** after onset of myocardial injury
• Repeat (serial troponin) at the interval required by the assay - this is why suspected NSTE-ACS is referred for **serial ECG + troponin**
• STEMI is diagnosed on ECG; do not wait for troponin
cards.m: Early troponin can be falsely reassuring.

cards.q: What is the initial assessment of suspected ACS in a Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **ABCDE approach**
• Assess **vital signs**
• Establish **IV access**
• **Continuous cardiac monitoring** if available; defibrillator nearby
• **12-lead ECG within 10 min**
cards.m: Stabilise, cannulate, monitor, ECG.

cards.q: What is the aspirin dose in suspected ACS, and why is it chewed?
cards.a:
• **Aspirin 300 mg** loading dose, **chewed** (non-enteric-coated)
• Chewing gives **buccal absorption and faster platelet inhibition**
• Then 75-150 mg daily
• Avoid only if true aspirin allergy or active major bleeding
cards.m: Chew 300 - the cheapest life-saving drug in the clinic.

cards.q: What is the clopidogrel loading dose in ACS, and what is the exception?
cards.a:
• **Clopidogrel 300 mg loading**, then **75 mg daily** (dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin)
• Exception: age **>75 years** (when fibrinolysis is planned) → **75 mg only, no loading dose** - reduces intracranial bleeding risk
• Primary PCI centres may use 600 mg
cards.m: Over 75 → give just 75.

cards.q: When is sublingual GTN given in ACS?
cards.a:
• **Sublingual GTN** if **chest pain persists or recurs**
• e.g. 0.5 mg SL, repeat every 5 min up to 3 doses if BP allows
• Relieves ischaemic pain by venodilatation (reduced preload) and coronary vasodilatation
• Check BP before each dose
cards.m: GTN for pain - but check the BP first.

cards.q: What are the contraindications to GTN in ACS?
cards.a:
• **SBP <90 mmHg** (or big drop from baseline)
• **PDE5 inhibitor** use: sildenafil/vardenafil within **24 h**, tadalafil within **48 h**
• Suspected **right ventricular infarction**
• **Severe aortic stenosis**, HR <50 or >100/min
cards.m: Low BP, Little blue pill, Right ventricle - no nitrates.

cards.q: When should oxygen be given in suspected ACS?
cards.a:
• Only if **hypoxaemic**: **SpO2 <90%** (some guidance <94%), aiming for **94-98%**
• **Routine oxygen in normoxic patients gives no benefit** and may enlarge the infarct (vasoconstriction)
• Note: slide says ‘give oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%’, which may be read as oxygen for all - correct practice is oxygen **only if SpO2 is low**
cards.m: Treat the saturation, not the diagnosis.

cards.q: How do you recognise right ventricular infarction, and what changes in management?
cards.a:
• Accompanies **inferior STEMI** (II, III, aVF); RCA occlusion
• Triad: **hypotension, raised JVP, clear lung fields**
• Confirm with **right-sided ECG - ST elevation in V4R**
• **Avoid GTN** and diuretics (preload dependent); give **IV fluid boluses** for hypotension
cards.m: Inferior MI + low BP + clear lungs → think RV, think fluids, not nitrates.

cards.q: How is STEMI on ECG referred from primary care?
cards.a:
• **Activate the STEMI pathway** (call the cardiac/ED hotline)
• **Immediate transfer to a PCI-capable centre** for **primary PCI** if appropriate
• Give aspirin + clopidogrel before transfer; if PCI cannot be done in time → fibrinolysis
cards.m: STEMI: don’t investigate, transfer.

cards.q: What are the key reperfusion time targets in STEMI?
cards.a:
• **Primary PCI** preferred if **first medical contact-to-device ≤120 min**
• **Door-to-balloon ≤90 min** at a PCI centre
• If PCI not achievable in time: **fibrinolysis**, **door-to-needle ≤30 min**
• Greatest benefit within **12 h** of symptom onset (best within 3 h)
cards.m: 30 for the needle, 90 for the balloon, 120 is the limit.

cards.q: What are the main contraindications to fibrinolysis (e.g. streptokinase) in STEMI?
cards.a:
• Absolute: any **previous intracranial haemorrhage**, **ischaemic stroke within 6 months**, intracranial neoplasm/AVM, **aortic dissection**, **active bleeding**/bleeding disorder, major trauma, surgery or head injury within **1 month**, GI bleed within 1 month
• **Streptokinase-specific**: **previous streptokinase exposure** (neutralising antibodies) and hypotension
cards.m: Brain bleed, recent stroke, dissection, bleeding - no clot-buster.

cards.q: How is suspected NSTE-ACS managed from a Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **Urgent hospital referral**
• Hospital does **serial ECG + troponin + risk assessment** (e.g. TIMI/GRACE)
• Before transfer: aspirin, clopidogrel, GTN if pain, oxygen only if hypoxic, IV access, monitoring
cards.m: No ST elevation does not mean no MI.

cards.q: Which features make an ACS 'unstable', and how is it transferred?
cards.a:
• **Cardiogenic shock**, **acute pulmonary oedema**, **significant arrhythmia**, **persistent chest pain**
• **Emergency transfer to the nearest appropriate hospital** for stabilisation
• Then subsequent transfer to a **PCI-capable centre**
cards.m: Unstable → nearest hospital first, PCI centre second.

cards.q: What must be done and communicated during transfer of an ACS patient?
cards.a:
• **Continue monitoring and supportive care** (ECG monitor, defibrillator, IV access, staff who can do CPR)
• **Send the ECG and relevant results**
• Inform the receiving team of **time of symptom onset** and **treatment given** (aspirin, clopidogrel, GTN times and doses)
cards.m: Send the patient, the ECG, the clock and the drug list.

cards.q: How is stroke defined?
cards.a:
• A clinical syndrome of **acute onset focal neurological deficit**
• Lasting **more than 24 hours** (or leading to death)
• Due to **cerebrovascular disease** - ischaemic (about 80%) or haemorrhagic (about 20%)
cards.m: Focal, sudden, vascular, >24 h.

cards.q: How does a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) differ from a stroke?
cards.a:
• **TIA**: focal deficit that **resolves within 24 h** (usually within 1 h) **without infarction** on imaging
• **Stroke**: deficit >24 h or infarct on imaging
• TIA is a **warning**: high early stroke risk - refer urgently for assessment and secondary prevention
cards.m: TIA = a stroke that gave you a warning.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for stroke?
cards.a:
• **Non-modifiable**: **age, male sex, family history of stroke**
• **Modifiable**: **hypertension** (most important), **diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, smoking, ischaemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation**
cards.m: AF throws clots to the brain; hypertension bursts and blocks vessels.

cards.q: What does 'time is brain' mean?
cards.a:
• In an acute large-vessel ischaemic stroke about **1.9 million neurons die every minute** untreated
• Benefit of thrombolysis/thrombectomy **falls steadily with time**
• So record onset time and **transfer immediately** - do not delay for tests in the clinic
cards.m: Every minute counts - two million neurons a minute.

cards.q: What does BE-FAST stand for in stroke recognition?
cards.a:
• **B**alance - sudden loss of balance/coordination
• **E**yes - sudden visual loss or double vision
• **F**ace drooping
• **A**rm (or leg) weakness
• **S**peech difficulty
• **T**ime - note onset and call 999 / transfer
cards.m: BE-FAST adds Balance and Eyes to FAST to catch posterior circulation strokes.

cards.q: Which associated symptoms may accompany stroke, and which suggest a haemorrhage?
cards.a:
• Associated: **severe headache, confusion, nausea, sensory impairment, bladder dysfunction**
• **Sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache, vomiting, reduced GCS, very high BP** → suspect **haemorrhagic stroke**
• Only CT can reliably distinguish ischaemia from haemorrhage
cards.m: Headache + vomiting + drowsy = think bleed, but scan to be sure.

cards.q: What does the general examination of a suspected stroke patient include?
cards.a:
• **Airway, Breathing, Circulation**
• Vital signs: **BP, HR, SpO2, temperature**
• **Capillary blood glucose**
• **Signs of trauma**
cards.m: ABC + glucose before anything neurological.

cards.q: What does the neurological examination in suspected stroke include?
cards.a:
• **Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)**
• **Cranial nerves**
• **Motor** and **sensory function**
• **Cerebellar function**
• **Gait**
cards.m: GCS, nerves, power, feeling, coordination, walking.

cards.q: What is the NIHSS used for, and what does it assess?
cards.a:
• **National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale** - determines **severity and location** of stroke (score 0-42)
• Domains: **level of consciousness, visual function, motor function, sensation and neglect, cerebellar function, language**
• Guides thrombolysis/thrombectomy decisions and tracks change
cards.m: NIHSS = a number for how bad the stroke is.

cards.q: What cardiac examination findings point to a cause of stroke?
cards.a:
• **Irregularly irregular pulse** → **atrial fibrillation** (cardioembolic)
• **Murmur** → valvular disease, infective endocarditis
• **Carotid bruit** → carotid stenosis
cards.m: Feel the pulse, listen to the heart, listen to the neck.

cards.q: Besides the heart, what else is examined in suspected stroke to find a cause or complication?
cards.a:
• **Head and neck**: contusion, laceration or deformity (trauma, possible subdural)
• **Fundoscopy**: hypertensive/diabetic retinopathy, papilloedema
• **Signs of infection** (e.g. endocarditis, meningitis)
• **Peripheral vascular disease** - marker of generalised atherosclerosis
cards.m: Look for the cause from head to toe.

cards.q: What are the acute investigations in suspected stroke?
cards.a:
• **Urgent non-contrast CT brain**
• **Full blood count** (platelets)
• **Renal profile**
• **Coagulation profile** (INR - e.g. on warfarin)
• **Blood glucose**
• These are the checks needed before thrombolysis
cards.m: CT + bloods that decide whether alteplase is safe.

cards.q: Why is an urgent non-contrast CT brain the first imaging in acute stroke?
cards.a:
• Clinical features **cannot reliably separate ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke**
• NCCT rapidly **excludes haemorrhage** (acute blood is bright without contrast)
• Haemorrhage must be excluded **before thrombolysis or antiplatelets**
• Early ischaemic changes may be absent - a normal CT does not exclude infarction
cards.m: CT answers one urgent question: bleed or no bleed?

cards.q: What cardiac investigations are done after stabilisation in ischaemic stroke?
cards.a:
• **ECG** (and Holter) - **atrial fibrillation**
• **Echocardiogram** - cardiac thrombus, valve disease, PFO
• **Carotid artery Doppler ultrasound** - carotid stenosis (candidate for endarterectomy)
cards.m: Find the source: rhythm, heart chambers, carotids.

cards.q: What risk-factor work-up is done after a stroke?
cards.a:
• **Fasting lipid profile**
• **HbA1c**
• **Thrombophilia screen** - mainly in **young stroke** or no obvious cause
• Plus BP monitoring for secondary prevention
cards.m: Fats, sugar, sticky blood.

cards.q: What are the three steps of pre-hospital stroke management in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Identify stroke**: FAST/BE-FAST; record **exact time of symptom onset**
• **Initial assessment**: ABC, **identify hypoglycaemia (stroke mimic)**, monitor vital signs
• **Urgent referral**: **immediate ambulance transfer** to a stroke-ready hospital within the **4.5-hour** thrombolysis window
cards.m: Spot it, stabilise it, ship it.

cards.q: Why must capillary glucose be checked in every suspected stroke?
cards.a:
• **Hypoglycaemia** can cause focal deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia) that **mimic stroke**
• It is **rapidly reversible** - give glucose and reassess
• Other mimics: post-ictal (**Todd’s paresis**), migraine with aura, sepsis, intracranial tumour, functional disorder
cards.m: Check the sugar before you call it a stroke.

cards.q: Why record the exact time of onset, and what if the patient woke up with symptoms?
cards.a:
• **Thrombolysis eligibility** depends on time from onset (within **4.5 h**)
• If onset was unwitnessed or on waking, use the **time last seen well**
• Ask relatives/witnesses; bring them along or get a phone number
cards.m: The clock starts when they were last normal, not when they were found.

cards.q: Where and how urgently should a patient with acute stroke be referred from a Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **Immediate ambulance transfer** (call MERS 999 / hospital)
• To a **stroke-ready hospital** capable of CT and thrombolysis
• Aim to arrive within the **4.5-hour window** from onset
• Pre-alert the receiving team with onset time and glucose
cards.m: Do not send a stroke home with a letter - send it in an ambulance.

cards.q: What is the dose and administration of IV alteplase for acute ischaemic stroke?
cards.a:
• Indication: onset **within 4.5 hours**, haemorrhage excluded on CT
• **Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg** (maximum **90 mg**)
• **10% as IV bolus** over 1 min, **remaining 90% infused over 1 hour**
cards.m: 0.9, 10% push, 90% over the hour.

cards.q: What is the dose of IV tenecteplase in acute ischaemic stroke, and its practical advantage?
cards.a:
• **Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg** (maximum **25 mg**)
• Given as a **single IV bolus** - no infusion needed
• Same 4.5-hour window; convenient before transfer for thrombectomy
cards.m: Tenecteplase - one shot.

cards.q: What is endovascular thrombectomy (EVT), and who is it for?
cards.a:
• Mechanical clot retrieval via catheter
• For **large vessel occlusion** of the **ICA or proximal MCA**
• Within **6 hours** of onset, and selected patients **up to 24 hours** using perfusion imaging
• Can be combined with IV thrombolysis
cards.m: Big clot, big vessel - pull it out.

cards.q: Should aspirin be given in the clinic to a patient with suspected acute stroke?
cards.a:
• **No** - not until **CT has excluded intracerebral haemorrhage**
• Aspirin would worsen a haemorrhagic stroke, and could delay thrombolysis decisions
• After haemorrhage excluded (and no thrombolysis): aspirin 300 mg within 48 h
• Contrast with ACS, where aspirin is given immediately
cards.m: Heart attack: aspirin now. Brain attack: CT first.

cards.q: How should high blood pressure be handled in acute stroke in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Do not lower BP aggressively** before transfer
• Raised BP maintains perfusion of the **ischaemic penumbra**; rapid falls extend the infarct
• Hospital targets: <185/110 before thrombolysis; otherwise treat only if very high (about >220/120)
• Also keep **nil by mouth** until swallow is screened
cards.m: The brain is borrowing that pressure - leave it.

cards.q: What are the three important families of snakes in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Elapidae** - cobras, king cobra, kraits, coral snakes, sea snakes
• **Viperidae** - true (Old World) vipers (Viperinae) and **pit vipers (Crotalinae)**
• **Natricidae (keelbacks)** - mostly harmless, except the **red-necked keelback**
• Source: MOH Malaysia Guideline: Management of Snakebite (2017)
Note: slide spells ‘Viparidae’ - correct spelling is **Viperidae**.
cards.m: E-V-K: Elapids paralyse, Vipers bleed, Keelbacks mostly harmless.

cards.q: Which Malaysian snakes belong to the Elapidae, and what is their main venom effect?
cards.a:
• **Cobras**: Naja kaouthia (monocled), Naja sumatrana (equatorial spitting)
• **King cobra**: Ophiophagus hannah
• **Kraits**: Malayan krait, banded krait
• **Coral snakes**, **sea snakes**
• Main effect: **neurotoxic** - descending flaccid paralysis (cobras also cause local necrosis; sea snakes myotoxicity)
cards.m: Elapids = Electric (nerve) venom.

cards.q: Which snakes belong to the Viperidae, and what is their main venom effect?
cards.a:
• **True vipers (Viperinae)** and **pit vipers (Crotalinae)** - pit = heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril
• Important Malaysian example: **Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma)**, northern Peninsular Malaysia
• Main effect: **haemotoxic** (venom-induced consumption coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia) + **cytotoxic** local swelling, blistering, necrosis
cards.m: Vipers = Vessels and blood.

cards.q: Which keelback snake is clinically important, and why?
cards.a:
• **Red-necked keelback (Rhabdophis subminiatus)**
• The **only keelback that can cause coagulopathy** (haematotoxic, like vipers)
• Most other keelbacks cause no significant harm
Note: slide spells it ‘subminitus’ - correct is **subminiatus**.
cards.m: Red neck = red flag among keelbacks.

cards.q: What history should be taken after a snake bite (WHEN, WHERE, HOW, WHAT)?
cards.a:
• **WHEN**: date and time of bite
• **WHERE**: geolocation; body part bitten
• **HOW**: activity before bite, snake on ground or tree, behaviour (hooding, spitting), number of strikes, snake escaped/captured/killed, description, **photo**
• **WHAT**: first aid done to the limb; **allergies, previous snakebite or antivenom, anaphylaxis**; occupational exposure (snake handlers)
cards.m: When, Where, How, What - the snakebite 4 W’s.

cards.q: Why ask about the snake’s behaviour and ask for a photograph?
cards.a:
• Helps **identify the species** → predicts the venom syndrome and choice of **monospecific antivenom**
• **Hooding or spitting** suggests a **cobra**
• Bite at night while asleep on the floor with little local pain suggests a **krait**
• Never try to catch or kill the snake - risk of further bites; dead snakes can still bite reflexly
cards.m: A photo is worth a thousand antivenom guesses.

cards.q: Why is a history of previous antivenom or allergy important in a snakebite patient?
cards.a:
• Antivenoms are **animal-derived (equine) immunoglobulins**
• Previous exposure, atopy or snake handler status increases the **risk of early anaphylactic reactions** to antivenom
• Antivenom is still given if indicated, with **adrenaline drawn up and ready**
cards.m: Horse serum before? Expect a reaction, prepare adrenaline.

cards.q: What is the first priority on examining a snakebite patient?
cards.a:
• **Airway and breathing**: respiratory effort, **bradypnoea**, upper airway compromise from **neurotoxic muscle weakness**
• Vitals: BP, HR, RR, SpO2, temperature, pain score, **GCS**
• Note early non-specific signs: nausea, vomiting, malaise, abdominal pain, drowsiness, collapse
cards.m: Neurotoxins kill by stopping breathing - check it first.

cards.q: What is looked for at the local bite site?
cards.a:
• **Fang/teeth puncture marks** - may be **absent or atypical**
• **Swelling, inflammation, bruising** (early sign of dermonecrosis), **blistering**
• **Tender, enlarged draining lymph nodes** - sign of venom absorption
cards.m: No fang marks does not mean no venom.

cards.q: How should progression of swelling after a snake bite be monitored?
cards.a:
• **Do not use permanent markers** - use **removable micropore tape strips** to label the advancing margin
• Mark the **distal border** at fixed intervals (every **2-3 hours**)
• Calculate the **Rate of Proximal Progression (RPP)** in **cm/hour**
• Rapidly progressive swelling is an indication for antivenom
cards.m: Tape the edge, time the spread.

cards.q: Why is measuring limb girth not recommended after a snake bite?
cards.a:
• Venom-induced swelling **moves proximally** along the limb
• It does not cause a fixed, localised compartmental swelling
• A girth at one fixed point misses the spread - use **Rate of Proximal Progression** instead
cards.m: Measure how far it travels, not how fat it gets.

cards.q: What is the earliest and most reliable sign of neurotoxic envenoming?
cards.a:
• **Ptosis**
• Followed by **descending flaccid paralysis**: external ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, dilated pupils, facial weakness
• Then **bulbar palsy** (dysphagia, pooled secretions, nasal voice, aphonia) → neck, limbs, respiratory muscles
• Caused by elapids: cobras, kraits, sea snakes
cards.m: It starts at the eyelids and descends to the diaphragm.

cards.q: What do the 'broken neck sign' and paradoxical abdominal breathing indicate after a snake bite?
cards.a:
• **Broken neck sign**: paralysis of **neck flexor muscles** - head cannot be lifted
• **Paradoxical abdominal respiration**: respiratory muscle weakness
• Both signal **impending respiratory arrest** from neurotoxic envenoming → airway support/intubation + urgent antivenom
cards.m: Floppy neck → failing breathing next.

cards.q: What are the signs of haematotoxic envenoming, and which snakes cause it?
cards.a:
• **Spontaneous bleeding**: continuous oozing from bite site and **venepuncture sites**, gum bleeding, epistaxis, conjunctival haemorrhage, petechiae
• Occult internal bleeding: haematuria, haematemesis, haemoptysis
• Caused by **vipers, pit vipers, red-necked keelback**
cards.m: Vipers make you ooze.

cards.q: What are the features of cytotoxic (local tissue) envenoming, and which snakes cause it?
cards.a:
• **Severe local pain**, **progressive oedema**
• **Blebs/blisters**
• **Purplish dermonecrosis**
• Caused by **cobras** and **pit vipers**
cards.m: Cobras and pit vipers digest the limb.

cards.q: What are the features of myotoxic envenoming (rhabdomyolysis), and which snakes cause it?
cards.a:
• Mainly **sea snakes**
• **Generalised muscle pain**, tenderness, stiffness, **trismus**
• **Dark brown urine (myoglobinuria)**
• **Hyperkalaemia** and **oliguric acute kidney injury**
cards.m: Sea snakes melt muscle → brown urine → high potassium.

cards.q: How often is the coagulation profile checked after a snake bite?
cards.a:
• **PT, aPTT, INR** at **baseline and 6-hourly** for **pit viper and unidentified bites**
• **D-dimer and fibrinogen** if coagulopathy is present
• **FBC**: serial Hb/Hct (occult bleeding), **platelets** (thrombocytopenia in pit viper envenoming)
cards.m: Pit viper or unknown snake: clot tests every 6 hours.

cards.q: Which investigations detect rhabdomyolysis and its complications after a sea snake bite?
cards.a:
• **Creatine kinase** - serial every **4-6 hours**
• **Renal profile and electrolytes** - creatinine, urea, **potassium** (AKI, hyperkalaemia)
• **Urine FEME** - myoglobinuria, haematuria, proteinuria
• ECG for hyperkalaemia
cards.m: CK, K+, creatinine, cola-coloured urine.

cards.q: Why are ECG and arterial blood gas monitored in envenomed patients?
cards.a:
• **ECG**: baseline and serial - **arrhythmias**, especially in **cobra (Naja) envenoming**; also hyperkalaemia
• **ABG**: **respiratory acidosis** from hypoventilation in neurotoxic paralysis, or **metabolic acidosis** in acute renal failure
• **LFT**: mild enzyme rise after severe local muscle damage
cards.m: Cobra hearts and paralysed lungs need monitoring.

cards.q: Which procedure is strictly contraindicated in suspected viper coagulopathy?
cards.a:
• **Arterial puncture** - risk of **uncontrollable haematoma**
• Also **avoid IM injections**
• Use peripheral venous samples from easily compressible sites
cards.m: Non-clotting blood + an artery = a haematoma you can’t stop.

cards.q: How is the 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) done and interpreted?
cards.a:
• Put **2 mL of venous blood** in a **new, clean, dry glass tube**
• Leave **undisturbed for 20 minutes**, then tilt once
• **Blood still liquid = coagulopathy** (venom-induced consumption coagulopathy) → indication for **antivenom**
• Simple bedside test where lab is unavailable; repeat **6-hourly**
cards.m: No clot at 20 minutes = viper venom at work.

cards.q: What is the first aid and primary care management of snake bite in a Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **Reassure**; keep patient **calm and still** to slow venom spread
• **Immobilise the bitten limb** with splint or sling in a **neutral position at heart level**
• **Avoid IM injections** if pit viper or coagulopathy suspected
• Remove rings/tight items; IV access in an unaffected limb
• **Urgent referral** to hospital
cards.m: Calm, still, splint - and send.

cards.q: Which traditional first-aid measures for snake bite are harmful and must be avoided?
cards.a:
• **Tight arterial tourniquets** - ischaemia, gangrene, sudden venom release when removed
• **Incision or cutting** the wound, **sucking** venom
• **Ice**, electric shock, herbal or chemical applications
• Delaying transfer to visit traditional healers
cards.m: No cut, no suck, no tie, no ice.

cards.q: Which snakebite patients need urgent referral and admission for observation?
cards.a:
• **Local and/or systemic envenoming** signs
• **Venomous snake** bite
• **Unidentified snake** bite
• **Unidentified animal** bite
• Observe for at least **24 hours** - krait and sea snake envenoming may be painless with **delayed onset**
cards.m: Venomous, envenomed, or unknown → admit.

cards.q: When can a patient bitten by a non-venomous snake be safely discharged?
cards.a:
• Snake **positively identified as non-venomous by a trained expert**, AND
• Clinical condition **matches the expected effect** of that species, AND
• **No significant tissue injury** (laceration, persistent bleeding) needing treatment
cards.m: Expert ID + matching clinical picture + no wound problem.

cards.q: What are the indications for antivenom after a snake bite?
cards.a:
• **Systemic envenoming**: spontaneous bleeding, **non-clotting 20WBCT**/abnormal coagulation, thrombocytopenia; **neurotoxic signs** (ptosis onwards); shock or arrhythmia; AKI; myoglobinuria
• **Severe local envenoming**: swelling of **more than half the bitten limb**, **rapid progression**, swelling after bites on digits
• Given **IV in hospital**, monospecific if species known, with **adrenaline ready**
cards.m: Antivenom treats envenoming, not the bite itself.

cards.q: What is the global burden of rabies?
cards.a:
• About **60,000 human deaths a year** worldwide
• **>95%** in **Asia and Africa**
• **>40%** of deaths in **children under 15 years**
• Almost all human cases come from **dog bites**; once symptomatic it is almost **100% fatal** - but fully preventable with PEP
cards.m: Rabies: 100% fatal, 100% preventable.

cards.q: What is the rabies situation in Malaysia, and why does the location of the bite matter?
cards.a:
• **Sarawak** is a **declared Rabies Infected Area** (outbreak since 2017)
• **Immune Belt**: gazetted border districts (Malaysia-Thailand border) where dogs are mass-vaccinated
• Rest of Peninsular Malaysia largely non-endemic
• Location decides the **risk level** and need for PEP
cards.m: Sarawak bite = rabies risk until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What types of exposure can transmit rabies?
cards.a:
• **Bite**
• **Scratch**
• **Lick on broken skin** or a scabless wound
• **Mucosal contact with saliva** (eyes, mouth, nose)
• Licks on intact skin do not transmit
cards.m: Saliva meets a break in the barrier.

cards.q: Why does it matter whether a dog bite was provoked or unprovoked?
cards.a:
• **Unprovoked attacks** carry a **higher rabies risk**
• So do **unusual bites by familiar pets** during routine feeding or petting
• A provoked bite (e.g. stepping on the dog, teasing) is more likely normal defensive behaviour
cards.m: A friendly dog that suddenly bites is a warning sign.

cards.q: Which animal factors are assessed after a dog bite?
cards.a:
• **Species and ownership**: dog, cat, bat, wild animal; confined pet vs free-roaming vs **stray**
• **Vaccination status**: anti-rabies vaccine **within the past 12 months**?
• **Availability for observation**: alive and observable for **14 days**, or missing, dead or culled?
• Do not delay PEP while waiting for the observation period
cards.m: Who owns it, is it vaccinated, can we watch it for 14 days?

cards.q: Which behaviours in the biting animal suggest rabies?
cards.a:
• **Furious**: sudden aggression, **unprovoked biting** of familiar people, **biting inanimate objects**, biting multiple humans/animals within 14 days
• **Dumb**: dull appearance, **ataxia**, aimless wandering
• Altered barking, poor appetite, **hypersalivation/frothing**
cards.m: Furious or dumb - both can be rabid.

cards.q: Which patient factors change rabies post-exposure management?
cards.a:
• **Prior rabies immunisation**: completed PrEP or previous PEP - dates and number of doses; was the last dose **<3 months or ≥3 months** ago
• Previously vaccinated: **booster vaccine only, no rabies immunoglobulin**
• **Immunocompromise**: HIV with low CD4, chemotherapy, systemic steroids, **chloroquine**, poorly controlled diabetes, congenital immunodeficiency → **full PEP including RIG** (poorer vaccine response)
cards.m: Vaccinated before → boost. Immunocompromised → give everything.

cards.q: What are the clinical phases of human rabies?
cards.a:
• **Prodromal**: fever, flu-like illness, fatigue, headache; **pain, paraesthesia, itching or numbness at the bite site**
• **Neurological (furious)**: hyperactivity, confusion, **hydrophobia** (spasm on swallowing liquids), **aerophobia**, convulsions
• **Paralytic**: **ascending flaccid paralysis starting from the bitten limb** → coma
• Incubation usually 1-3 months (days to over a year)
cards.m: Tingling at the old bite + fear of water = rabies.

cards.q: Which bite sites carry the highest rabies risk, and why?
cards.a:
• **Head, neck, face, hands, genitalia** - **rich nerve supply** and short path to the CNS
• Risk without PEP: **head 55%**, upper extremity 22%, lower limb 12%, trunk 9%
• **Multiple bites** increase risk
• These high-risk sites shorten incubation - start PEP immediately
cards.m: Closer to the brain, richer in nerves = faster and riskier.

cards.q: Can rabies be diagnosed in a bitten person before symptoms appear?
cards.a:
• **No** - **no diagnostic test detects human rabies during the incubation period**
• So PEP decisions are based on **exposure risk**, never on testing the patient
• Symptomatic (ante-mortem) tests: **nuchal skin biopsy**, serial **saliva, CSF and urine rRT-PCR**
cards.m: You cannot test your way out of PEP.

cards.q: What is the gold standard laboratory test for rabies in the animal?
cards.a:
• **Direct fluorescent antibody test (DFA/FAT)** on **brain tissue** - medulla and cerebellum
• **Negri body** histology is **no longer recommended** for routine diagnosis (insensitive)
• Arranged through the District Veterinary Office
cards.m: FAT on the brain, not Negri on the slide.

cards.q: What is the single most critical step in primary care management of a dog bite?
cards.a:
• **Immediate local wound care**
• **Flush and wash** with **running water and soap/detergent for at least 15 minutes**
• Then apply **povidone-iodine or 70% alcohol**
• Do this even if the patient presents late
cards.m: Wash for 15 - it physically removes and kills the virus.

cards.q: Should dog bite wounds be sutured?
cards.a:
• **Avoid primary suturing** - it may inoculate virus deeper into neural tissue and traps bacteria
• If suturing is unavoidable (e.g. large facial wound): **delay**, keep sutures loose, and **infiltrate RIG first**
Note: slide says ‘avoid secondary suturing’; the standard advice is to **avoid primary (immediate) suturing**.
cards.m: Leave dog bites open - sew later, if ever.

cards.q: What adjunctive treatment is given for a dog bite wound in addition to wound washing?
cards.a:
• **Tetanus toxoid** (ATT) according to immunisation status; tetanus immunoglobulin for dirty wounds in the unimmunised
• **Empirical oral antibiotics** - **amoxicillin-clavulanate** - for **deep puncture or contaminated wounds** (and hand, face, delayed presentation, immunocompromised)
cards.m: Every bite: think Tetanus, Antibiotics, Rabies.

cards.q: What notification and referral are required after an animal bite in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Fill in the **Animal Bite Notification Form** within **24 hours**
• Notify the **District Health Office (DHO)** and **District Veterinary Office (DVO)**
• **Refer Category II and III exposures** to hospital for rabies PEP
cards.m: Bite → form in 24 h → DHO + DVO.

cards.q: What are the WHO categories of rabies exposure and the PEP for each?
cards.a:
• **Category I**: touching/feeding animals, **licks on intact skin** → **no PEP** (wash)
• **Category II**: **nibbling** of uncovered skin, **minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding** → wound care + **vaccine**
• **Category III**: **transdermal bites or scratches**, **licks on broken skin**, **mucosal contamination with saliva**, any **bat** exposure → wound care + **vaccine + rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)**
cards.m: I = intact, II = scratch (vaccine), III = blood (vaccine + RIG).

cards.q: How is rabies post-exposure prophylaxis given to an unvaccinated person?
cards.a:
• **Vaccine** (WHO regimens): IM **days 0, 3, 7 and one dose between day 14-28**, or intradermal 2 sites on **days 0, 3, 7**
• **RIG** for Category III: human RIG **20 IU/kg** (equine 40 IU/kg), **infiltrated into and around the wound** as much as possible, once, up to day 7 of vaccination
• Never give RIG in the same syringe or site as vaccine
cards.m: RIG neutralises now; vaccine protects later.

cards.q: What organism causes rapid infection after a cat bite, and why are cat bites high risk?
cards.a:
• **Pasteurella multocida** - symptoms within **12-24 hours** (very rapid onset)
• Cat teeth are thin and sharp → **deep punctures** into tendon sheaths, joints and bone
• Infection rate much higher than dog bites (about **30-50%**)
• Spread by bites, scratches, licks on broken skin, kissing pets, contaminated fomites (e.g. pacifiers)
cards.m: Cat bite: small hole, deep trouble, fast.

cards.q: What are the manifestations and treatment of Pasteurella multocida infection?
cards.a:
• Soft tissue infection at the bite; **bone and joint infection** (septic arthritis, osteomyelitis); respiratory infection; invasive disease - meningitis, bacteraemia, endocarditis, peritonitis
• **Prophylaxis** for deep or delayed wounds: **amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5 days**
• **Established infection**: swab, then **amoxicillin-clavulanate**; if penicillin-allergic, **doxycycline or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole**
Note: slide lists metronidazole + doxycycline/ciprofloxacin as the treatment; this is the **penicillin-allergy alternative**, not first line. Flucloxacillin, cephalexin and erythromycin cover Pasteurella poorly.
cards.m: Pasteurella loves Penicillin (co-amoxiclav).

cards.q: What is cat scratch disease, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Bartonella henselae** - from scratches, bites, cat saliva and **cat fleas (Ctenocephalides felis)**; kittens commonest source
• **Slower onset**: papule/vesicle at inoculation site, then **tender regional lymphadenopathy** 1-3 weeks later
• **Benign, self-limiting** (weeks to months)
• **Warm compresses**; for unresolved lymphadenopathy a macrolide - slide: **erythromycin 10 days** (azithromycin 5 days is a common alternative)
cards.m: Pasteurella = fast and furious; Bartonella = slow and swollen nodes.

cards.q: How common are jellyfish stings worldwide?
cards.a:
• Up to **150 million jellyfish stings** occur worldwide each year
• Most are mild and local; a few species (box jellyfish) can kill within minutes
cards.m: Very common, usually trivial, occasionally lethal.

cards.q: How does a jellyfish sting cause injury?
cards.a:
• Tentacle contact exposes skin to **nematocysts** (venom-injecting stinging cells)
• Nematocysts **discharge and inject venom** into the skin
• Venom causes **local irritation, pain and inflammation**
• In severe cases **systemic effects** on multiple organs - can be life-threatening
cards.m: Nematocysts = microscopic harpoons loaded with venom.

cards.q: Which jellyfish are dangerous, and what can box jellyfish envenomation do?
cards.a:
• **Portuguese man-o’-war (Physalia physalis)**
• **Box jellyfish** (cubozoans; found in Malaysian waters)
• Severe box jellyfish envenomation: **tissue necrosis, severe pain and death within minutes** (cardiorespiratory arrest)
cards.m: Box jellyfish - the deadliest box at the beach.

cards.q: What is the classic skin sign of a jellyfish sting?
cards.a:
• **Tentacle prints**: **linear red urticarial lesions** (whip-like streaks) where tentacles touched
• Box jellyfish may leave a **ladder-like, cross-hatched** pattern
• Wide areas of tentacle contact predict more venom and systemic risk
cards.m: Lines on the skin = tentacles were there.

cards.q: What are the mild symptoms of a jellyfish sting, and what do they depend on?
cards.a:
• Depend on **species, amount of venom injected and area of skin** affected
• Mild: **local pain, itching, burning or throbbing**
• **Rash** with red, purple or brown patches
cards.m: Pain, itch, burn, rash - local only.

cards.q: What are the red-flag (severe) symptoms after a jellyfish sting?
cards.a:
• **Respiratory**: difficulty breathing
• **Cardiovascular**: chest pain
• **Neurological**: numbness or tingling
• **Musculoskeletal**: muscle cramps
• **GI**: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
• Skin blisters; excessive sweating, difficulty swallowing
• Any red flag → resuscitate and transfer to ED
cards.m: Anything beyond the skin = systemic = emergency.

cards.q: How is hot water immersion used for jellyfish stings?
cards.a:
• Immerse or shower the area in **hot water at 40-45°C** (hot but tolerable - test with unaffected hand)
• Usually about **20 minutes** or until pain settles (slide: up to 90 min)
• **Inactivates the heat-labile venom** and gives **better pain relief** than acetic acid, papain or opioids
cards.m: Heat kills the venom protein - hot, not boiling.

cards.q: What is the role of vinegar (acetic acid) in jellyfish stings?
cards.a:
• Douse with **household vinegar (4-5% acetic acid)** for at least 30 s, especially for **box jellyfish**
• It **inactivates undischarged nematocysts** on the skin, preventing further venom injection
• It is **not an analgesic** - pain is treated with hot water, analgesia ± **IV morphine**
Note: slide lists acetic acid under analgesics; its real role is to **stop further nematocyst firing**.
cards.m: Vinegar disarms; hot water and morphine relieve.

cards.q: What is Irukandji syndrome?
cards.a:
• Envenomation by a tiny box jellyfish, **Carukia barnesi**
• Mild sting, then after **20-40 min**: severe **back and abdominal pain, muscle cramps, sweating, anxiety, vomiting**
• **Catecholamine surge** → **hypertension, tachycardia**, cardiomyopathy, pulmonary oedema
• Can lead to **cardiac arrest and death** - needs hospital (opioids, BP control)
cards.m: Small sting, huge adrenaline storm, delayed.

cards.q: What must NOT be done after a jellyfish sting?
cards.a:
• **Do not rinse with fresh water** - osmotic change makes nematocysts fire
• **Do not rub** with sand or towels
• **Do not apply urine** or alcohol
• Instead: leave the water, call for help, CPR if needed, vinegar, **lift off tentacles with tweezers or gloved hand**, then hot water
cards.m: No fresh water, no rubbing, no urine.

cards.q: What history is taken after a bee or wasp sting?
cards.a:
• **Time, site and number of stings**
• **Bee or wasp** if known (Hymenoptera venom allergy)
• **Previous sting reaction / known venom allergy**
• Local pain, erythema, swelling
• **Anaphylaxis symptoms**: urticaria/angioedema, throat tightness, wheeze/dyspnoea, dizziness/syncope, abdominal symptoms
cards.m: How many, which insect, reacted before, any systemic symptoms?

cards.q: What is a large local reaction to an insect sting?
cards.a:
• Swelling **beyond the sting site**, **>10 cm** in diameter, lasting **>24 hours** (peaks at 24-48 h)
• **Not anaphylaxis** - no systemic features
• Low risk of future anaphylaxis; treat with cold compress, antihistamine ± short steroid course
Note: slide writes ‘>10, >24 hours’ without units; the threshold is **10 cm**.
cards.m: 10 cm, 24 hours - big but local.

cards.q: When is a sting reaction anaphylaxis?
cards.a:
• Acute onset (minutes to hours) of **skin/mucosal features** (urticaria, angioedema) **plus** respiratory compromise or **hypotension/collapse**
• Or **two or more systems** involved (skin, respiratory, circulatory, GI) after a likely allergen
• Or **hypotension** alone after a known allergen
• Skin signs are absent in up to 10-20%
cards.m: Airway, Breathing or Circulation problem + allergen = anaphylaxis.

cards.q: What is examined in a patient stung by a bee or wasp?
cards.a:
• **ABCDE + vital signs + SpO2**
• **Airway**: facial/tongue swelling, **hoarseness, stridor**
• **Breathing**: wheeze, respiratory distress
• **Circulation**: hypotension, shock
• Skin: generalised urticaria/angioedema; sting site and extent of swelling
cards.m: Hoarse voice or stridor = airway closing.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment and adult dose for anaphylaxis?
cards.a:
• **IM adrenaline STAT** - the only first-line drug
• Adult: **0.5 mg IM** = **0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000)**
• **Anterolateral thigh**
• Antihistamines and steroids are **adjuncts only** - never delay adrenaline for them
cards.m: Anaphylaxis: Adrenaline, Adrenaline, Adrenaline.

cards.q: What is the IM adrenaline dose for a child with anaphylaxis? (e.g. 20 kg child)
cards.a:
• **0.01 mg/kg IM**, **maximum 0.5 mg**
• Using **1 mg/mL (1:1000)**: 0.01 mL/kg
• 20 kg child → **0.2 mg = 0.2 mL** of 1:1000, anterolateral thigh
• Repeat after **5 minutes** if no improvement
cards.m: 0.01 per kilo - for 1:1000 the mg and the mL are the same number.

cards.q: Why is IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis given into the anterolateral thigh?
cards.a:
• **Vastus lateralis** is large and well perfused → **faster absorption and higher peak levels** than deltoid or subcutaneous injection
• **IM, not IV bolus** in primary care - IV bolus risks arrhythmias and hypertension
• Can be given through clothing in an emergency
cards.m: Thigh is fastest - and IM is safest.

cards.q: When is IM adrenaline repeated in anaphylaxis?
cards.a:
• **Repeat after 5 minutes** if symptoms persist or worsen
• Can be repeated every 5 min; after 2 doses with ongoing shock/bronchospasm → refractory anaphylaxis, needs ED/ICU (adrenaline infusion)
• Keep monitoring cardiac rhythm, BP and SpO2
cards.m: Re-dose every 5 minutes until better.

cards.q: What supportive measures accompany adrenaline in anaphylaxis?
cards.a:
• **Supine with legs elevated** (sit up if breathless; left lateral if pregnant); **never stand them up suddenly**
• **High-flow oxygen**
• **IV access + IV crystalloid bolus if hypotensive** (adult 500-1000 mL; child 10-20 mL/kg)
• **Monitor** cardiac rhythm, BP, SpO2
• **Nebulised salbutamol** for persistent bronchospasm
cards.m: Lie flat, legs up, oxygen, fluids, nebuliser.

cards.q: How is a local or large local reaction to a sting managed?
cards.a:
• **Remove any retained bee stinger**
• **Cold compress**
• **Analgesia ± oral antihistamine**
• Consider a **short course of oral corticosteroids** for severe swelling
• No adrenaline needed if no systemic features
cards.m: Local reaction: scrape, cool, soothe.

cards.q: When must a patient with a bee or wasp sting be transferred urgently to the Emergency Department?
cards.a:
• **Anaphylaxis** (after IM adrenaline is given in the KK)
• **Airway compromise** or **respiratory distress**
• **Persistent hypotension** or **circulatory collapse**
• **Multiple stings** with **systemic toxicity**
cards.m: Refer the ABCs: Anaphylaxis, Breathing/airway, Circulation, plus the swarm (many stings).

cards.q: Which sting patients need referral to an Allergy/Immunology service, and why?
cards.a:
• Anyone with a **previous systemic (venom-mediated) allergic reaction** to a sting
• Purpose: **venom allergy testing** and assessment for **venom immunotherapy (VIT)**
• VIT = graded desensitisation that greatly **reduces the risk of future anaphylaxis**
• Large local reactions alone usually do **not** need VIT
cards.m: Systemic once → specialist once: VIT turns a deadly sting into a nuisance.

cards.q: Bee vs wasp sting: how does the stinger differ, and how should a retained bee stinger be removed?
cards.a:
• **Honeybee**: barbed stinger with venom sac is **left in the skin**; bee dies; one sting
• **Wasp**: smooth stinger, **not left behind**; can sting **repeatedly**
• Remove a bee stinger **as fast as possible** (venom keeps pumping for about a minute)
• **Scrape** it out sideways with a fingernail or card edge, or pluck quickly - speed matters more than method
• Then **cold compress** and analgesia
cards.m: Bee leaves its barb; wasp walks away armed.

cards.q: What should be arranged for a patient recovering from sting-induced anaphylaxis before discharge from care?
cards.a:
• Hospital **observation** (risk of **biphasic reaction** hours later)
• Prescribe an **adrenaline auto-injector** and teach its use (thigh, through clothing)
• Written **anaphylaxis action plan**; **medical alert** card/bracelet; record allergy in clinic notes
• **Avoidance** advice (shoes outdoors, no sweet drinks or perfume outdoors, care near nests)
• Referral to **Allergy/Immunology** for venom immunotherapy
cards.m: Leave with the 3 As: Auto-injector, Action plan, Allergy referral.

cards.q: What labour history is taken from a woman presenting to a KK in labour?
cards.a:
• **Gestational age** and **parity**
• **Contractions**: onset, frequency and duration
• **Show** or **vaginal bleeding**
• **Leaking liquor**: onset, amount and **colour**
• **Fetal movements**
cards.m: Labour history = the 4 Ls: Length of pregnancy, Labour pains, Leaking (liquor/blood), Life (fetal movements).

cards.q: Which obstetric risk factors must be checked in the history of a woman in labour?
cards.a:
• **Previous Caesarean section / uterine surgery** (scar rupture risk)
• **Previous obstetric complications** (e.g. PPH, shoulder dystocia)
• **Current pregnancy complications** or **medical illness** (e.g. hypertension, diabetes, anaemia)
• **Review the antenatal record** (home-based card) and the **planned place and mode of delivery**
cards.m: Scar, Past, Present, Plan.

cards.q: What maternal general examination is done for a woman in labour?
cards.a:
• **General condition** and **vital signs**: BP, pulse, temperature, RR ± SpO₂
• Look for **pallor** (anaemia: poor PPH tolerance)
• Look for **oedema** (pre-eclampsia)
• Look for **signs of distress** or exhaustion

cards.q: What is assessed on abdominal examination of a woman in labour?
cards.a:
• **Fundal height** (correlate with dates)
• **Lie** and **presentation**
• **Engagement** of the presenting part (fifths palpable)
• **Fetal heart rate**
• **Contractions**: frequency, duration and strength
cards.m: Height, Lie, Head (engagement), Heart, Hardening (contractions).

cards.q: What does a vaginal examination in labour assess, and when is it done?
cards.a:
• Done **only if indicated** (and never before excluding placenta praevia when there is bleeding)
• **Cervical dilatation** and **effacement**
• **Presenting part**, **position** and **station**
• **Membranes**: intact or ruptured
• **Liquor**: colour (clear vs meconium/blood) and amount
cards.m: No VE in APH until praevia is excluded.

cards.q: What are the four steps of intrapartum management in a KK?
cards.a:
• 1. **Assess maternal and fetal wellbeing**: vital signs, fetal heart rate, contractions/progress, high-risk features
• 2. **Determine the stage of labour**: latent vs active; start labour documentation
• 3. **Supportive care**: reassurance, continuous support, companion, pain relief, hydration
• 4. If **high-risk/complication**: **stabilise** the mother, **monitor** mother and fetus, arrange **urgent hospital transfer**
cards.m: Assess → Stage → Support → Stabilise & send.

cards.q: What is the difference between latent and active labour, and why does it matter in a KK?
cards.a:
• **Latent phase**: irregular-to-regular contractions with cervical change **up to 4 cm**; can be slow
• **Active phase**: cervix **≥ 4 cm** with regular painful contractions
• Latent phase: monitor with the **Labour Progress Chart**
• Active phase: **commence the partograph**; a KK without delivery capability should refer
cards.m: 4 cm is the gate: Progress Chart before, Partograph after.

cards.q: What supportive care is given to a woman in labour?
cards.a:
• **Reassurance** and **continuous support**
• Allow a **companion** where appropriate
• **Appropriate pain relief** (non-drug measures, Entonox, pethidine as available)
• Maintain **hydration** according to clinical condition (oral fluids if low risk)
cards.m: Continuous support shortens labour and lowers interventions - it is treatment, not kindness only.

cards.q: Which maternal features in labour mandate urgent referral to hospital?
cards.a:
• **Maternal instability**
• **BP ≥ 140/90** (pre-eclampsia risk)
• **Fever** (chorioamnionitis/sepsis)
• **Significant medical disease** (e.g. cardiac disease, diabetes)
• **Antepartum or intrapartum bleeding**
cards.m: Mother sick, hot, high or bleeding → hospital.

cards.q: What fetal heart rate in labour is abnormal and needs urgent referral?
cards.a:
• Normal FHR: **110-160 bpm**
• **< 110** (bradycardia) or **> 160** (tachycardia) = abnormal → **urgent referral**
• Suggests **fetal hypoxia/distress** (tachycardia may also mean maternal fever/infection)
• While arranging transfer: left lateral position, oxygen if hypoxic, IV fluids, stop oxytocics
cards.m: Fetal heart lives between 110 and 160.

cards.q: Why is meconium-stained liquor in labour an indication for urgent referral?
cards.a:
• May indicate **fetal hypoxia/distress** (hypoxia triggers gut peristalsis and sphincter relaxation)
• Risk of **meconium aspiration syndrome** in the newborn
• Needs **continuous fetal monitoring** and a **neonatal resuscitation** team at delivery
• Thick, dark green meconium is more worrying than thin, light staining
cards.m: Green liquor = red flag.

cards.q: How should cord prolapse be managed in a KK while arranging transfer?
cards.a:
• **Call for help**; arrange **emergency transfer** for immediate delivery (usually Caesarean)
• Relieve cord compression: **manually push the presenting part up** or **fill the bladder** (500-750 mL saline via Foley)
• Position **knee-chest** or **exaggerated left lateral (Sims)**
• **Minimal handling** of the cord (spasm); keep it inside or warm and moist
• Monitor fetal heart
cards.m: Lift the baby off the cord - do not play with the cord.

cards.q: Which presentation, gestation and membrane/progress problems in labour need urgent hospital referral?
cards.a:
• **Breech, transverse lie** or other **malpresentation**
• **Preterm labour < 37 weeks** (neonatal care, steroids if < 34 weeks)
• **Prolonged rupture of membranes** (> 18 h: chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis risk)
• **Abnormal labour progress**
cards.m: Wrong way, too early, too long - refer.

cards.q: What is the Labour Progress Chart (LPC) and what is recorded on it in a KK?
cards.a:
• Used at the **KK in early (latent) labour**, before the partograph
• Records **maternal vital signs**
• **Fetal heart rate**
• **Uterine contractions**
• **Pad/liquor observation**
• Supports **serial clinical reassessment** to detect progress or problems

cards.q: When is the partograph started, and what should a KK without delivery capability do?
cards.a:
• **Commence the partograph** once **active labour** is reached (cervix **≥ 4 cm**)
• A KK **without delivery capability**, or any **high-risk labour**: **assess, stabilise and refer** to hospital
• Do not keep active labour in a clinic not set up for delivery
cards.m: Active labour + no labour room = ambulance.

cards.q: How are the alert and action lines of the WHO partograph used?
cards.a:
• Plotting of **cervical dilatation** starts at the **alert line** (expected **1 cm per hour** from 4 cm)
• Crossing the **alert line** = slow progress → in a health clinic, **refer** to hospital
• **Action line** is drawn **4 hours to the right** of the alert line
• Crossing the action line → **intervention** needed (assess for obstruction, augmentation or Caesarean)
cards.m: Alert = arrange transfer; Action = act now.

cards.q: How is the third stage of labour actively managed if a baby is delivered in a KK?
cards.a:
• **Oxytocin 10 IU IM** within **1 minute** of birth (after excluding another baby)
• **Delayed cord clamping** about 1-3 minutes if the baby is well
• **Controlled cord traction** with counter-pressure above the pubis
• **Uterine massage** after the placenta is delivered; check placenta is **complete**
• Prevents **postpartum haemorrhage** (most common cause: uterine atony)
cards.m: AMTSL = Oxytocin, Traction, Massage (O-T-M).

cards.q: What is the first-line management of postpartum haemorrhage after a delivery in a KK?
cards.a:
• **Call for help**; ABC, **2 large-bore IV cannulae**, bloods/group and crossmatch, **IV crystalloid**
• **Rub up the uterus** (fundal massage) and **empty the bladder**
• **Uterotonics**: oxytocin infusion; ergometrine (avoid if hypertensive)
• Consider **IV tranexamic acid 1 g** within 3 hours of birth
• Check placenta and genital tract for **tears**; **bimanual compression** if atonic; urgent transfer
cards.m: 4 Ts of PPH: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin.

cards.q: What is a seizure, and is every fit epilepsy?
cards.a:
• **Seizure**: a **transient** occurrence of signs/symptoms due to **abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity** in the brain
• **NOT every fit = epilepsy**
• Common mimics: **syncope** (brief jerks with fainting), **hypoglycaemia**, **psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES)**
• **Epilepsy** = tendency to recurrent **unprovoked** seizures
cards.m: Fit is a symptom; epilepsy is a diagnosis.

cards.q: Focal vs generalised seizure: what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Focal**: starts in **one area** (one hemisphere); may have **impaired awareness**; may spread to become bilateral
• **Generalised**: involves **both hemispheres from onset**, e.g. **tonic-clonic**, absence, myoclonic
• A focal onset (aura, one-sided jerking, head/eye deviation) points to a **structural cause** - look for one
cards.m: Focal = one spot; Generalised = whole brain from the go.

cards.q: What are the common causes of seizures in children?
cards.a:
• **Fever / febrile seizure** (commonest; age 6 months-5 years)
• **CNS infection** (meningitis, encephalitis)
• **Metabolic** (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia)
• **Poisoning / ingestion**
• **Epilepsy / neurological disorder**
• **Trauma** (including non-accidental injury)
cards.m: Fever first - but never forget meningitis behind a febrile fit.

cards.q: What are the common causes of seizures in adults?
cards.a:
• **Missed anti-seizure medication** (commonest in known epilepsy)
• **Stroke / structural lesion** (tumour, bleed)
• **Metabolic** (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia)
• **Alcohol / drugs** (including withdrawal)
• **CNS infection**
• **Trauma**
• Note: the slide repeats 'medication stroke / structural' - a copy-paste duplication
cards.m: Adults: Missed meds, Mass/stroke, Metabolic, Mind-altering substances, Meningitis, Mechanical trauma (6 Ms).

cards.q: What is asked about the period BEFORE a seizure?
cards.a:
• **Fever**
• **Trauma** (head injury)
• **Drugs / alcohol** (intake or withdrawal)
• **Missed anti-epileptic drugs**
• **Previous seizures**
• Also triggers and warning (aura, standing up, pain - favours syncope)
cards.m: Before: was it Provoked? (fever, fall, drink, drug missed).

cards.q: What features are asked about DURING a seizure (from the eyewitness)?
cards.a:
• **Loss of consciousness**
• **Eye / head deviation**
• **Jerking** or **stiffening**
• **Focal** vs **generalised** movements
• **Tongue bite** (lateral) and **incontinence**
• **Duration** - get a timed account
cards.m: Ask the witness, film it if possible: a phone video is worth a thousand descriptions.

cards.q: What features are asked about AFTER a seizure, and what is Todd's paresis?
cards.a:
• **Post-ictal confusion** and **time to return to baseline**
• **Headache**, drowsiness, muscle aches
• **Todd's paresis**: transient **weakness** of a limb after a focal seizure, resolving within hours (up to 48 h)
• Prolonged confusion favours seizure over syncope (rapid recovery)
cards.m: Todd's paresis = the brain's 'tired' side; if it does not recover, think stroke.

cards.q: What additional history is taken for a child with a seizure?
cards.a:
• **Fever** (febrile seizure vs CNS infection)
• **Birth history** (prematurity, hypoxic injury)
• **Development** (delay suggests underlying neurological disorder)
• **Ingestion** of drugs or poisons
• **Family history** of seizures or febrile fits
cards.m: Paeds extra history = Fever, Birth, Development, Ingestion, Family (FBDIF).

cards.q: How is a seizing or post-ictal patient assessed using ABCDE?
cards.a:
• **A**: airway patent? **secretions**?
• **B**: RR, **SpO₂**, cyanosis
• **C**: HR, BP, CRT, **IV access**
• **D**: **GCS**, **pupils**, **glucose**, neurological examination
• **E**: **temperature**, trauma, **rash**, **meningism**
cards.m: In D, Don't Ever Forget Glucose (DEFG).

cards.q: Why must capillary glucose be checked early in every fitting patient, and what other reversible causes are sought?
cards.a:
• **Hypoglycaemia** causes seizures and is **rapidly reversible** (IV dextrose, e.g. 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg in children)
• Benzodiazepines will not fix a hypoglycaemic fit
• Other reversible causes: **infection**, **electrolyte abnormality**, **trauma**, **toxins**
cards.m: Glucose before diazepam: sugar is the fastest anticonvulsant in a hypo.

cards.q: What should be done during an active seizure?
cards.a:
• **Protect from injury** (move hazards, cushion the head)
• **Maintain the airway**; suction secretions
• **Oxygen if hypoxic**
• **Position safely** (on the side when possible)
• **IV access**; **monitor ECG and SpO₂**
• **Correct reversible causes** (e.g. hypoglycaemia)
• **Note the time** of onset
cards.m: Protect, Position, Oxygen, Time it.

cards.q: What is done after the seizure stops?
cards.a:
• **Recovery position**
• **Reassess ABC**
• **Repeat neurological examination** (GCS, pupils, focal deficit)
• **Continue observation** until back to baseline
• **Identify the underlying cause**
cards.m: After the storm: Recover, Reassess, Re-examine, Reason why.

cards.q: How is status epilepticus defined for treatment purposes?
cards.a:
• Seizure lasting **> 5 minutes**, or
• **Recurrent seizures without recovery** of consciousness in between
• At 5 minutes a seizure is unlikely to stop on its own → **give a benzodiazepine** without waiting
• Ongoing status (about 30 minutes) risks **permanent neuronal injury**
cards.m: 5 minutes = treat; do not wait for 30.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment of a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, and what are the usual doses?
cards.a:
• **Benzodiazepine** first line
• **IV lorazepam** 0.1 mg/kg (max **4 mg**)
• **IV diazepam** 0.2-0.3 mg/kg (max **10 mg**)
• **No IV access**: **buccal or intranasal midazolam** 0.3 mg/kg (max **10 mg**), or **rectal diazepam** 0.5 mg/kg (max 10 mg)
• Note: slide spells 'benzodiadepine' and 'intranasl' - correct: benzodiazepine, intranasal
cards.m: No line? Use the cheek (buccal midazolam) or the bottom (rectal diazepam).
