cards.q: What is the next step if a seizure continues after the first benzodiazepine dose?
cards.a:
• **Repeat one dose** of benzodiazepine after about 5 minutes (**maximum 2 doses** in total)
• More doses risk **respiratory depression**
• **Prepare urgent transfer** to hospital (ambulance with oxygen, monitoring)
• Hospital second line: **IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg**, **levetiracetam** or **valproate**
cards.m: Two benzos, then the big guns in hospital.

cards.q: What are the do's and don'ts for a seizing patient?
cards.a:
• **Do**: protect the airway, **time** the seizure, check **ABC**, check **glucose**
• **Don't restrain** the patient
• **Don't put anything in the mouth** (spoons, fingers - broken teeth, aspiration, bitten fingers)
• **Don't force the mouth open**
cards.m: Nothing in the mouth: you cannot swallow your tongue.

cards.q: Which seizure presentations need IMMEDIATE referral to hospital?
cards.a:
• **Status epilepticus**
• **First unprovoked seizure**
• **Recurrent seizures without recovery**
• **Persistent GCS < 15** or **focal neurological deficit**
• Suspected **meningitis/encephalitis**
• **Significant head injury**
• **Persistent hypoglycaemia** or **respiratory compromise**
cards.m: Immediate: not stopping, not waking, not normal, or not the first time it is unexplained.

cards.q: Which special groups with seizures need immediate referral, and what is the key drug for a fit in late pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Pregnancy**: a fit after 20 weeks or postpartum = **eclampsia** until proven otherwise → **IV magnesium sulphate** (4 g loading slowly over 10-15 min, then 1 g/h), control BP, urgent transfer
• **Infant < 6 months** with a seizure (febrile seizures are unusual this young: think infection, metabolic)
• **Complex febrile seizure** with concerning features (focal, > 15 min, or recurrent within 24 h)
cards.m: Pregnant fit = magnesium, not just diazepam.

cards.q: Which seizure patients need URGENT (not immediate) referral to a specialist?
cards.a:
• **New diagnosis of epilepsy**
• **Uncontrolled seizures despite medication**
• **Suspected intracranial pathology**
• **Persistent post-ictal deficit**
• **Diagnostic uncertainty** (e.g. seizure vs syncope vs PNES)
cards.m: Urgent = needs a neurologist soon, not an ambulance now.

cards.q: When is a patient who had a seizure suitable for discharge from the clinic?
cards.a:
• Seizure **resolved completely**
• **Returned to baseline neurological status**
• **Cause identified and managed**
• **No red flags**
• **Responsible caregiver** available
• **Clear follow-up** arranged (plus safety advice: no driving, no swimming alone)
cards.m: Discharge only when all six boxes are ticked.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man collapses in the waiting area of a Klinik Kesihatan. He does not respond to a shoulder tap or a loud voice. After you shout for help and the resuscitation trolley, you open his airway: he makes occasional gasping breaths and you cannot feel a carotid pulse within 10 seconds.
What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Start chest compressions at 100-120 per minute, 30:2 with breaths
Give one rescue breath every 6 seconds and recheck pulse in 2 minutes
Place him in the recovery position because he is still breathing
Feel for the carotid pulse for a further 30 seconds to be certain
Give five initial rescue breaths, then reassess for signs of life
mcq.e: Occasional gasping is **agonal breathing**, a sign of cardiac arrest, not of adequate breathing. With no normal breathing and no pulse after a check of **no more than 10 seconds**, start high-quality compressions at once. Prolonged pulse checks and recovery positioning only delay CPR; five initial rescue breaths belong to paediatric, not adult, BLS.
w: Correct - agonal gasps plus no pulse means cardiac arrest: compress immediately at 30:2.
Wrong - rescue breathing alone is for a patient who has a pulse but is not breathing normally.
Wrong - gasping is not normal breathing; recovery position would leave an arrested heart untreated.
Wrong - the pulse check must not exceed 10 seconds; every extra second is no-flow time.
Wrong - five initial rescue breaths are a paediatric step; adults start with compressions.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man is carried into a KK after being found unresponsive in a public toilet with a syringe beside him. He has a strong carotid pulse of 96/min but is not breathing. A bag-valve-mask is ready.
What is the most appropriate ventilation plan while awaiting help?
o: Start chest compressions and breaths at a ratio of 30:2
Give one breath every 6 seconds, about 10 breaths per minute
Give one breath every 3 seconds, about 20 breaths per minute
Place him in the recovery position and observe his breathing
Give two breaths every 30 seconds until the ambulance arrives
mcq.e: With a **definite pulse but absent or abnormal breathing**, the slides advise rescue breathing alone: **1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min)**, each over 1 second with visible chest rise, rechecking the pulse every 2 minutes. Compressions are for a pulseless patient. Faster rates cause hyperventilation and gastric inflation; naloxone, if available, is an add-on and not a substitute for ventilation.
w: Wrong - he has a strong pulse, so compressions are not indicated.
Correct - pulse present but no breathing: 1 breath every 6 s (10/min) with pulse checks every 2 min.
Wrong - 20 breaths/min is hyperventilation, raising intrathoracic pressure and inflating the stomach.
Wrong - the recovery position suits a patient who is breathing normally; he is apnoeic.
Wrong - 4 breaths per minute is far too few and he will become profoundly hypoxic.

mcq.stem:
During a mock code in a KK, a medical officer watches a staff nurse perform chest compressions on an adult manikin connected to a feedback device.
Which pattern meets the criteria for high-quality CPR?
o: Depth 4-5 cm at 100-120/min, keeping the hands pressed between beats
Depth 6-7 cm at 120-140/min, with full recoil after every compression
Depth 5-6 cm at 100-120/min, with full recoil after every compression
Depth 5-6 cm at 80-100/min, with full recoil after every compression
Depth 5-6 cm at 100-120/min, pausing 15 seconds every cycle for checks
mcq.e: High-quality adult CPR means the **lower half of the sternum**, depth **at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm**, rate **100-120/min**, **complete recoil**, minimal interruptions and 30:2. Leaning prevents recoil and cardiac refilling, compressing too fast reduces depth and filling time, and pauses of more than 10 seconds drop coronary perfusion pressure to zero.
w: Wrong - 4-5 cm is too shallow and leaning on the chest prevents recoil and venous refilling.
Wrong - deeper than 6 cm risks injury and faster than 120/min shortens filling time.
Correct - 5-6 cm, 100-120/min and full recoil are the core targets of high-quality CPR.
Wrong - 80-100/min is below the minimum rate of 100 per minute.
Wrong - interruptions must be minimised; routine 15-second pauses every cycle are harmful.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man has a witnessed cardiac arrest in a KK car park. CPR is in progress and a colleague arrives with an AED. His chest is bare and dry.
Where should the two electrode pads be placed?
o: One pad on the upper sternum and one directly over the lower sternum
One pad below the left clavicle and one below the right clavicle
Both pads on the left anterior chest, a hand's breadth apart
One pad below the right clavicle and one over the cardiac apex
One pad on the left upper back and one over the right lower ribs
mcq.e: Standard anterolateral placement puts the first pad on the **right upper chest below the clavicle** and the second over the **apex** (left mid-axillary line, V6 level), so current crosses the bulk of the ventricles. Pads close together or both on the same side let current run across the skin instead of through the heart. Anteroposterior placement is an alternative, but it pairs the left precordium with the left back.
w: Wrong - both pads on the sternum are too close; current bypasses most of the ventricles.
Wrong - two infraclavicular pads lie above the heart and miss the ventricular mass.
Wrong - pads on the same side of the chest shunt current along the chest wall.
Correct - right infraclavicular plus apical pad gives the standard current path through the heart.
Wrong - this is not a recognised vector; the posterior pad goes on the left back with the anterior pad on the left chest.

mcq.stem:
In a KK treatment room, an AED analyses a collapsed 52-year-old woman and advises a shock. The shock is delivered after everyone is clear.
What should the team do immediately afterwards?
o: Check the carotid pulse for 10 seconds before deciding the next step
Press analyse again at once to confirm the rhythm has been converted
Give two rescue breaths, then look for normal breathing for 10 seconds
Wait for the AED voice prompt to confirm return of spontaneous circulation
Restart CPR with chest compressions straight away for about 2 minutes
mcq.e: After a shock, **resume CPR immediately, starting with compressions**; the AED re-analyses after about 2 minutes (5 cycles), when breathing and pulse are also reassessed. Even after successful defibrillation the stunned myocardium produces little output at first, so pausing to feel a pulse or re-analyse only lengthens no-flow time.
w: Wrong - an immediate pulse check delays compressions and is usually falsely negative.
Wrong - the AED re-analyses after 2 minutes of CPR, not immediately after a shock.
Wrong - compressions, not breaths, restart first, and reassessment waits for 2 minutes.
Wrong - the AED cannot confirm ROSC; waiting for prompts means doing nothing.
Correct - compressions restart at once and continue for 2 minutes before the next analysis.

mcq.stem:
Two nurses are performing CPR on an adult in a rural KK while waiting for the ambulance. After about 3 minutes, the compressor's depth on the feedback device starts to fall below 5 cm, although she says she is not tired.
What is the recommended practice for changing the person doing compressions?
o: Swap only when the compressor says that she is exhausted
Swap every 30 compressions so that each rescuer stays fresh
Swap every 5 cycles or 2 minutes, keeping the pause under 10 s
Swap every 10 minutes, at the pulse check after 25 cycles
Swap every minute, pausing CPR for 20 seconds to change places
mcq.e: Compression quality falls within 1-2 minutes even when the rescuer does not feel tired, so the slides advise switching **every 5 cycles or 2 minutes**, ideally at the rhythm check, with the change done in **under 10 seconds**. Waiting for exhaustion lets shallow compressions go unnoticed; changing too often multiplies interruptions.
w: Wrong - fatigue reduces depth before the rescuer notices it, as in this scenario.
Wrong - swapping after every cycle creates too many pauses in compressions.
Correct - change every 5 cycles or 2 minutes with a pause of less than 10 seconds.
Wrong - 10 minutes is far too long; depth will already have fallen.
Wrong - 20-second pauses every minute badly reduce coronary perfusion.

mcq.stem:
A medical officer and one nurse in a rural KK have been performing CPR on a 70-year-old man for 15 minutes. The AED keeps advising 'no shock'. The ambulance is still 20 minutes away.
Which of the following is an accepted reason to stop resuscitation?
o: The AED has advised no shock on three analyses in a row
His pupils are found to be fixed and dilated on checking
Fifteen minutes of CPR have passed without any response
The ambulance has been delayed and is still far from the KK
He opens his eyes, moves and starts to breathe normally
mcq.e: The slides list when CPR may stop: the **victim recovers** (wakes, moves, opens eyes, breathes normally), the **rescuers are exhausted**, or **trained help arrives** to take over. A 'no shock' message means a non-shockable rhythm or a perfusing rhythm, so CPR continues. Fixed pupils and an arbitrary time limit are not reliable stopping rules on their own.
w: Wrong - 'no shock' means a non-shockable rhythm (asystole/PEA); CPR must continue.
Wrong - pupils may be fixed during CPR or from drugs and do not on their own justify stopping.
Wrong - 15 minutes is not, by itself, a reason to stop basic life support.
Wrong - a delayed ambulance is a reason to keep going and rotate rescuers, not to stop.
Correct - signs of recovery such as waking, moving and normal breathing are a reason to stop CPR.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man who smells strongly of alcohol is found lying on the floor outside a KK. He does not respond to voice or a shoulder tap, but he is breathing normally at 16/min with a good radial pulse. There is no suggestion of trauma.
How should he be positioned while help is obtained?
o: Recovery position on his side, checking his breathing regularly
Supine with head tilt-chin lift and compressions ready to start
Sitting upright against the wall so gravity keeps the airway open
Prone with the head turned to one side and arms beside the body
Supine flat with a pillow under his head to keep him comfortable
mcq.e: An **unresponsive patient who is breathing normally** goes into the **recovery position**: the tongue falls forward and vomit drains out of the mouth, protecting the airway. Keep re-checking breathing and be ready to roll him back and start CPR if breathing becomes abnormal. A pillow under the head flexes the neck and promotes obstruction and aspiration.
w: Correct - recovery position protects the airway of an unresponsive but breathing patient.
Wrong - he has normal breathing and a pulse; he needs airway protection, not CPR.
Wrong - an unconscious patient slumps forward when sitting, obstructing the airway.
Wrong - the prone position restricts breathing and hides the face and airway from view.
Wrong - lying flat with a pillow lets the tongue fall back and vomit be aspirated.

mcq.stem:
Walking home from the KK, a nurse finds a man collapsed on the roadside. The area is safe. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Nobody else is around, but she has her mobile phone.
What should she do next?
o: Run to the nearest shop to look for an AED before starting CPR
Do two minutes of CPR first, then stop to telephone for help
Give five rescue breaths, then check for a pulse for 1 minute
Dial 999 on loudspeaker and start CPR while speaking to them
Put him in the recovery position, then go and call an ambulance
mcq.e: For out-of-hospital arrest, a **lone responder with a mobile phone dials MERS 999** and **starts CPR**, using the loudspeaker so calling and compressions happen together; the dispatcher can coach her and send help. Leaving the victim to fetch an AED delays CPR, and the recovery position is for patients who are breathing normally.
w: Wrong - leaving to find an AED leaves the victim with no circulation; send someone else if available.
Wrong - with a phone in hand there is no need to delay the call; do both at once.
Wrong - adult BLS starts with compressions and pulse checks must not exceed 10 seconds.
Correct - call 999 on speaker and start compressions without delay.
Wrong - he is not breathing normally, so he needs CPR, not the recovery position.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old motorcyclist is brought into a KK after a high-speed crash. He is unresponsive with snoring respiration and a palpable pulse. No cervical collar has been applied yet.
Which airway-opening manoeuvre is most appropriate?
o: Head tilt-chin lift with the neck fully extended on a pillow
Jaw thrust, pushing the angles of the mandible upwards
Blind finger sweep to clear the pharynx before positioning
Log-roll into the recovery position to let the tongue fall
Head tilt-chin lift with the face turned towards one side
mcq.e: In suspected **cervical spine injury**, the **jaw thrust** opens the airway by lifting the mandible forward without extending the neck. Head tilt-chin lift extends the spine and is used only if the jaw thrust fails, because a patent airway takes priority. Blind finger sweeps can push debris deeper.
w: Wrong - full neck extension could worsen an unstable cervical spine injury.
Correct - jaw thrust opens the airway while keeping the neck neutral.
Wrong - blind finger sweeps can push material deeper and injure the pharynx.
Wrong - repositioning does not reliably open the airway and is not the first manoeuvre here.
Wrong - head tilt with neck rotation still moves an injured spine.

mcq.stem:
During a resuscitation in a KK, a house officer squeezes the bag-valve-mask forcefully about 30 times a minute while compressions are in progress.
What is the main harmful effect of this ventilation pattern?
o: Respiratory acidosis that makes defibrillation less effective
Carbon dioxide retention that causes cerebral vasodilatation
Tension pneumothorax, which is the usual result in adults
Hypoxaemia because each breath is too short to oxygenate
Raised intrathoracic pressure that lowers venous return
mcq.e: Over-ventilation **raises intrathoracic pressure**, reducing **venous return** and therefore the cardiac output and coronary perfusion that compressions produce; it also inflates the stomach and risks regurgitation. Each breath should take **1 second** with just visible chest rise. Hyperventilation lowers CO2 rather than retaining it.
w: Wrong - hyperventilation causes alkalosis, not acidosis.
Wrong - excessive ventilation lowers CO2; it does not cause retention.
Wrong - barotrauma can occur but is not the usual or main harm.
Wrong - oxygenation is not the problem; the problem is reduced circulation.
Correct - high intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and coronary perfusion during CPR.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to a KK after being pulled from a pond. He is unresponsive, not breathing and has no pulse. Two trained nurses are present and five initial rescue breaths have been given.
What compression technique should they use?
o: 15:2, depth one-third of the chest's front-to-back diameter
30:2, depth 5-6 cm, the same as for an adult casualty
15:2, depth about 2 cm, using two fingers on the sternum
30:2, depth one-third of the chest's front-to-back diameter
5:1, depth one-half of the chest's front-to-back diameter
mcq.e: Children usually have **hypoxic arrests**, so paediatric BLS begins with **5 rescue breaths** and, with two rescuers, uses **15:2**. Compress the lower sternum to at least **one-third of the anteroposterior depth** (about 5 cm in a child, 4 cm in an infant). 30:2 is the lone lay-rescuer ratio, and two-finger compressions are for infants.
w: Correct - two-rescuer paediatric CPR is 15:2 to one-third of chest depth.
Wrong - adult ratio and depth ignore the hypoxic cause of paediatric arrest.
Wrong - 2 cm is far too shallow and two-finger technique is for infants.
Wrong - 30:2 is the single-rescuer ratio; two healthcare rescuers use 15:2.
Wrong - 5:1 is outdated, and half the chest depth is too deep.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man at a KK staff lunch suddenly clutches his throat while eating chicken. He is red-faced, coughing forcefully and says 'something went down the wrong way'.
What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Encourage him to keep coughing and watch closely
Sweep a finger blindly around the back of his throat
Lay him flat and start chest compressions at once
mcq.e: A patient who can **speak, breathe and cough forcefully** has a mild partial obstruction; his own cough is more effective than any manoeuvre, so **encourage coughing** and stay with him. Back blows and abdominal thrusts start only when the cough becomes **ineffective**, because they can worsen the obstruction or cause injury.
w: Wrong - back blows are reserved for an ineffective cough.
Wrong - abdominal thrusts come after failed back blows and can cause internal injury.
Correct - an effective cough clears the airway best; encourage it and monitor.
Wrong - blind finger sweeps can push the bolus further down.
Wrong - he is conscious and moving air; CPR is only for an unconscious victim.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old woman choking on a fish ball in the KK canteen cannot speak, her cough is now weak and silent, and she is becoming cyanosed. She is still conscious and standing.
What should be done first?
o: Up to 5 abdominal thrusts between the umbilicus and ribs
Up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades
Up to 5 chest compressions while she is still standing
Two rescue breaths to try to push the bolus downwards
A blind finger sweep to hook the food out of her throat
mcq.e: When the cough becomes **ineffective** in a conscious adult, the slide sequence is **up to 5 back blows first**, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, then keep **alternating 5 and 5**. Back blows come first because they work often and carry less risk of internal injury than abdominal thrusts.
w: Wrong - abdominal thrusts follow failed back blows.
Correct - back blows are the first manoeuvre once the cough is ineffective.
Wrong - compressions are started only after she becomes unconscious.
Wrong - rescue breaths cannot be given to a conscious standing patient and will not clear the bolus.
Wrong - blind finger sweeps risk impacting the object further.

mcq.stem:
Despite alternating back blows and abdominal thrusts, a 60-year-old choking man becomes unresponsive. You lower him to the floor and a colleague calls for help. When you open his airway, no object can be seen in his mouth.
What is the next step?
o: Continue abdominal thrusts with him lying supine on the floor
Perform a blind finger sweep to search for the foreign body
Roll him onto his side and give five more firm back blows
Start CPR, looking in the mouth each time breaths are given
Wait for him to breathe again before any further manoeuvre
mcq.e: Once a choking victim becomes **unconscious, start CPR**: chest compressions generate higher airway pressures than thrusts and may expel the object. Each time the airway is opened for breaths, look in the mouth and remove an object **only if it is visible**. **Blind finger sweeps are avoided** because they can push the object deeper.
w: Wrong - for an unconscious victim the slides move to CPR, not further thrusts.
Wrong - a blind sweep can impact the object and injure the pharynx.
Wrong - back blows are for conscious victims; he now needs compressions.
Correct - start CPR and remove the object only when it can be seen.
Wrong - he will not start breathing on his own while the airway is obstructed.

mcq.stem:
A mother rushes into a KK with her 8-month-old son, who was eating a piece of apple. He is conscious but cannot cry or cough effectively and is turning blue.
What is the correct first-aid sequence?
o: 5 back blows face down along the forearm, then 5 chest thrusts
5 back blows face down along the forearm, then 5 abdominal thrusts
5 abdominal thrusts with him sitting up, then 5 back blows
A blind finger sweep, then 5 back blows if nothing is found
Hold him upside down by the ankles and shake him firmly
mcq.e: In infants under 1 year, **abdominal thrusts are avoided** because the liver and spleen are large and poorly protected. Give **up to 5 back blows** with the head lower than the chest, then **up to 5 chest thrusts** (two fingers on the lower sternum), and repeat. Blind finger sweeps and dangling the infant are dangerous.
w: Correct - infants get back blows alternating with chest thrusts.
Wrong - abdominal thrusts can rupture the infant liver or spleen.
Wrong - abdominal thrusts are not used in infants and back blows come first.
Wrong - blind finger sweeps can push the food further in.
Wrong - shaking by the ankles risks injury and is not recommended.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation is choking at a KK antenatal clinic. Five back blows have not dislodged the food and her cough remains ineffective. She is still conscious.
What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?
o: Abdominal thrusts with the fist placed just above the umbilicus
Abdominal thrusts with the fist placed just below the umbilicus
Another 10 back blows before trying any other manoeuvre
Lie her in left lateral tilt and start chest compressions
Chest thrusts with the fist on the lower half of the sternum
mcq.e: In **late pregnancy** (and in marked obesity) abdominal thrusts are ineffective and risk injury to the uterus and fetus, so **chest thrusts** on the lower sternum replace them, alternating with back blows. CPR with left uterine displacement is started only if she becomes unconscious.
w: Wrong - the gravid uterus fills the abdomen; thrusts risk uterine and fetal injury.
Wrong - below the umbilicus is the wrong site in anyone and directly compresses the uterus.
Wrong - after 5 failed back blows, move to the next manoeuvre rather than repeating blows only.
Wrong - she is conscious; compressions are started only if she becomes unresponsive.
Correct - chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy and obesity.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old woman with diabetes presents to a KK with 1 hour of epigastric discomfort, nausea and sweating. BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 58/min. ECG shows 2-3 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF with ST depression in I and aVL.
Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
o: Left anterior descending artery
Left circumflex, obtuse marginal branch
Right coronary artery
Left main stem
First diagonal branch of the LAD
mcq.e: ST elevation in **II, III and aVF** is an **inferior STEMI**, most often due to **right coronary artery** occlusion; the RCA also supplies the SA and AV nodes (explaining the bradycardia) and the right ventricle, so record right-sided leads (V4R). Reciprocal depression in I and aVL supports the diagnosis. Diabetics, women and the elderly often present atypically with epigastric pain and nausea.
w: Wrong - LAD occlusion causes anterior ST elevation in V1-V4.
Wrong - circumflex occlusion usually gives lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6) or posterior changes.
Correct - inferior ST elevation with bradycardia points to the right coronary artery.
Wrong - left main occlusion gives widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR and shock.
Wrong - a diagonal branch gives high lateral changes in I and aVL, not inferior elevation.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old smoker walks up to a KK triage counter complaining of 30 minutes of central chest heaviness radiating to the left jaw, with sweating. BP 146/90 mmHg, HR 98/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
What is the most appropriate first investigation, and when?
o: Point-of-care troponin, with an ECG once the result is back
A 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact
A chest radiograph within 30 minutes to exclude dissection
A 12-lead ECG within 60 minutes, once he has seen the doctor
Fasting lipid profile and glucose before the doctor sees him
mcq.e: In suspected ACS, a **12-lead ECG** must be recorded and read **within 10 minutes of first medical contact**, because it immediately separates STEMI (needs reperfusion now) from NSTE-ACS. Troponin may be normal in the first hours and must never delay the ECG or referral. Lipids and glucose belong to the later work-up.
w: Wrong - troponin may be normal early and must not delay the ECG.
Correct - the ECG within 10 minutes is the key first test in suspected ACS.
Wrong - a chest film does not diagnose STEMI and must not come before the ECG.
Wrong - the ECG is done at triage, not after a delay for medical review.
Wrong - risk-factor bloods do not change immediate management.

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man in a KK has an ECG showing anterior ST elevation. He has no aspirin allergy and no active bleeding. The STEMI pathway has been activated and transfer is being arranged.
Which antiplatelet loading regimen do the slides recommend for him?
o: Aspirin 300 mg chewed plus clopidogrel 300 mg
Aspirin 300 mg chewed plus clopidogrel 600 mg
Aspirin 150 mg chewed plus clopidogrel 75 mg
Aspirin 300 mg chewed plus clopidogrel 75 mg
Aspirin 75 mg chewed plus clopidogrel 300 mg
mcq.e: **Aspirin 300 mg** is chewed for rapid absorption. The slides give **clopidogrel 300 mg** loading then 75 mg daily, but only **75 mg (no 300 mg load) in patients over 75 years**, because bleeding risk, including intracranial haemorrhage with fibrinolysis, rises steeply with age. Lower aspirin doses act too slowly as a loading dose.
w: Wrong - the 300 mg clopidogrel load is for patients aged 75 or younger.
Wrong - 600 mg is a cath-lab loading dose for primary PCI, not the slide regimen for an 80-year-old.
Wrong - 150 mg aspirin is an inadequate loading dose.
Correct - aspirin 300 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg because he is over 75 years old.
Wrong - 75 mg aspirin is a maintenance, not a loading, dose.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a KK with 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain. The ECG shows ST depression in V4-V6. BP 132/84 mmHg, HR 92/min. He took sildenafil 50 mg last night. Aspirin has been given and the pain persists.
Which medication should be withheld?
o: Clopidogrel 300 mg oral loading dose
Intravenous morphine titrated to pain
Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 94%
Atorvastatin 80 mg as a high-dose statin
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 0.5 mg
mcq.e: Nitrates with a **PDE-5 inhibitor** (sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours) cause profound, refractory hypotension because both raise cGMP and vasodilate. Other GTN contraindications are **SBP below 90 mmHg** and suspected **right ventricular infarction**. The slides give SL GTN for persistent pain, so always ask about erectile dysfunction drugs first.
w: Wrong - clopidogrel is part of the dual antiplatelet loading and is safe here.
Wrong - titrated morphine is acceptable for pain not relieved by other measures.
Wrong - oxygen guided by saturation is appropriate.
Wrong - a high-intensity statin is appropriate early in ACS.
Correct - GTN within 24 hours of sildenafil can cause severe refractory hypotension.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old man at a KK has ST elevation in II, III and aVF, and also in V4R. BP 84/56 mmHg, HR 62/min, JVP raised, lungs clear, SpO2 96%. The ambulance has been called.
What is the most appropriate immediate measure while awaiting transfer?
o: Cautious IV crystalloid bolus with close BP and chest monitoring
Sublingual GTN 0.5 mg repeated every 5 minutes for the pain
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg for the raised jugular venous pressure
High-flow oxygen 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask for all patients
Oral atenolol 50 mg to reduce the myocardial oxygen demand
mcq.e: Inferior STEMI with **hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs** plus ST elevation in V4R suggests **right ventricular infarction**. The RV depends on preload, so give **cautious fluid** and avoid preload-reducing drugs such as nitrates and diuretics. Hypotension also makes this unstable ACS, needing emergency transfer to the nearest appropriate hospital.
w: Correct - the preload-dependent right ventricle needs careful fluid loading.
Wrong - GTN is contraindicated with SBP below 90 mmHg and RV infarction.
Wrong - the raised JVP is from RV failure; diuresis drops preload and BP further.
Wrong - his SpO2 is 96%; oxygen is guided by saturation, not given to all.
Wrong - a beta-blocker in hypotension and borderline bradycardia can precipitate shock.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old woman with suspected NSTE-ACS is being prepared for transfer from a KK. She is comfortable at rest, RR 16/min, chest clear and SpO2 98% on room air.
What is the most appropriate oxygen plan?
o: Nasal prongs at 2 L/min routinely for every patient with ACS
Non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min to maximise myocardial oxygen
Venturi mask at 28% to keep the saturation close to 100%
No supplemental oxygen; monitor SpO2 and start if it falls
Oxygen only during the ambulance journey, then stop on arrival
mcq.e: Routine oxygen in normoxic ACS gives no benefit, and hyperoxia may cause coronary vasoconstriction. The slides target **SpO2 above 94%**, so oxygen starts only when saturation drops below that (MOH and ESC guidance use a lower threshold of about 90%). With SpO2 of 98%, **monitor and give oxygen only if hypoxic**.
w: Wrong - routine low-flow oxygen in normoxic patients is no longer recommended.
Wrong - high-flow oxygen gives no benefit and hyperoxia may harm the myocardium.
Wrong - aiming for 100% is unnecessary; she is already well saturated.
Correct - she is normoxic, so monitor SpO2 and give oxygen only if it falls.
Wrong - transfer is not an indication for oxygen; the saturation decides.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man in a KK has had ongoing chest pain for 1 hour. The ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V1-V4. Aspirin and clopidogrel have been given. A PCI-capable hospital is 40 minutes away by ambulance.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat the ECG and a troponin in 3 hours, then decide on referral
Activate the STEMI pathway for immediate transfer to a PCI centre
Observe in the KK for 2 hours to see if the GTN settles the pain
Refer to the medical outpatient clinic for a review tomorrow
Send him by private car with a referral letter to the nearest ED
mcq.e: **STEMI on the ECG** in a KK means **activating the STEMI pathway** for immediate ambulance transfer to a **PCI-capable centre** (primary PCI target about 90-120 minutes from first contact; fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be achieved in time). During transfer continue monitoring, send the ECG and results, and state the onset time and treatment given. Waiting for troponin only loses myocardium.
w: Wrong - STEMI is diagnosed on the ECG; troponin must not delay reperfusion.
Correct - ST elevation triggers the STEMI pathway and urgent transfer for PCI.
Wrong - observing in the KK delays reperfusion while muscle dies.
Wrong - an outpatient appointment for an acute STEMI could be fatal.
Wrong - he needs a monitored ambulance with a defibrillator, not a private car.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man with hypertension had 25 minutes of central chest tightness at rest this morning, which has now settled. In the KK he is pain-free, BP 138/82 mmHg, and his ECG shows 1 mm horizontal ST depression in V5-V6.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Discharge with sublingual GTN and an exercise ECG next month
Activate the STEMI pathway for primary PCI at the nearest centre
Urgent hospital referral for serial ECGs, troponin and risk scoring
Start a statin and review him in the KK in one week with lipids
Repeat the ECG in the KK tomorrow morning before deciding further
mcq.e: Rest pain with **ST depression** is suspected **NSTE-ACS** (unstable angina or NSTEMI). The slides advise **urgent hospital referral** for **serial ECG, troponin and risk assessment**; being pain-free does not exclude NSTEMI. The STEMI pathway is for ST elevation or new LBBB, and outpatient testing of an acute coronary syndrome is unsafe.
w: Wrong - an exercise test in a recent ACS is dangerous and delays diagnosis.
Wrong - there is no ST elevation, so the STEMI pathway is not triggered.
Correct - suspected NSTE-ACS needs urgent hospital referral for serial ECG and troponin.
Wrong - he needs same-day assessment, not KK follow-up in a week.
Wrong - delaying a day risks infarction or arrhythmia at home.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman in a rural KK has an anterior STEMI. She is now cold and clammy with BP 78/50 mmHg, bibasal crackles and SpO2 88%. The PCI-capable centre is 3 hours away; a district hospital is 25 minutes away.
What is the most appropriate referral plan?
o: Emergency transfer to the district hospital for stabilisation first
Direct 3-hour transfer to the PCI centre, bypassing the hospital
Keep her in the KK until the BP improves, then send to PCI centre
Arrange a cardiology clinic appointment once she has stabilised
Give sublingual GTN for the crackles, then transfer by private car
mcq.e: **Unstable ACS** - cardiogenic shock, acute pulmonary oedema, significant arrhythmia or persistent pain - needs **emergency transfer to the nearest appropriate hospital** for stabilisation, followed by transfer to a PCI-capable centre. A 3-hour journey in shock risks death en route. GTN is contraindicated with SBP below 90 mmHg.
w: Correct - unstable ACS goes to the nearest appropriate hospital first, then to PCI.
Wrong - a long journey in cardiogenic shock without stabilisation is unsafe.
Wrong - a KK cannot stabilise cardiogenic shock; waiting wastes time.
Wrong - this is an emergency, not a clinic referral.
Wrong - GTN with SBP 78 mmHg worsens shock, and a private car is unsafe.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to a KK with 1 hour of typical ischaemic chest pain and sweating. His ECG shows broad QRS complexes (140 ms) with a left bundle branch block pattern; a tracing 6 months ago was normal.
How should this ECG be interpreted?
o: A non-specific conduction delay that needs only outpatient review
Probable stable angina, as the pain is the only abnormal finding
A rate-related artefact; repeat once the heart rate has settled
Evidence of an old infarct that does not change today's plan
A STEMI equivalent; manage it on the STEMI pathway
mcq.e: **New LBBB** with ischaemic symptoms is listed on the slides among the ECG changes of ACS and is treated as a **STEMI equivalent**, because LBBB masks ST elevation from a large anterior infarct. Always compare with an old ECG: a known chronic LBBB is interpreted more cautiously.
w: Wrong - a new LBBB with ischaemic pain is not a benign finding.
Wrong - pain at rest with a new ECG change is acute, not stable angina.
Wrong - rate-related bundle branch block is uncommon and cannot be assumed here.
Wrong - the previous ECG was normal, so this is new, not old.
Correct - new LBBB with typical pain is managed as STEMI.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with an inferior MI four days ago presents to a KK with sudden severe breathlessness. HR 112/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, widespread crackles. There is a new loud pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, with no thrill.
What is the most likely complication?
o: Ventricular septal rupture
Pericarditis with tamponade
Left ventricular aneurysm
Papillary muscle rupture
Pulmonary embolism
mcq.e: A new **apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla** with **acute pulmonary oedema** a few days after MI suggests **acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture**; the posteromedial papillary muscle has a single (RCA) blood supply, so it is typical of inferior MI. Ventricular septal rupture also gives a pansystolic murmur, but at the left sternal edge, often with a thrill. Both are surgical emergencies.
w: Wrong - VSR gives a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, usually with a thrill.
Wrong - tamponade gives hypotension, raised JVP and soft heart sounds, not a new murmur.
Wrong - an aneurysm presents weeks later with persistent ST elevation, heart failure or emboli.
Correct - apical murmur to the axilla plus acute pulmonary oedema after inferior MI.
Wrong - PE does not cause a new apical pansystolic murmur and crackles.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide is brought to a KK with right-sided weakness and slurred speech noticed 40 minutes ago. BP 168/94 mmHg, SpO2 97%. He is drowsy and sweaty.
Which bedside test is most important before labelling this a stroke?
o: 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation
Capillary blood glucose by fingerprick
Urine dipstick for glucose and ketones
Pulse oximetry repeated on both hands
Body temperature to exclude sepsis
mcq.e: **Hypoglycaemia** is the classic **stroke mimic** and can cause focal weakness and dysarthria, especially with sulphonylureas or insulin; sweating and drowsiness are clues. The slides include blood glucose in the initial assessment, and it takes seconds to check and correct. An ECG for AF helps find a cause but does not exclude a mimic.
w: Wrong - an ECG finds a cause of stroke but does not rule out a mimic.
Correct - hypoglycaemia mimics stroke and must be excluded at once.
Wrong - urine glucose does not reflect the current blood glucose.
Wrong - his SpO2 is already normal; hypoxia is not the issue.
Wrong - sepsis is less likely and does not explain sudden focal deficits.

mcq.stem:
A 65-year-old woman developed sudden left facial droop, left arm weakness and slurred speech while gardening 1 hour ago. Capillary glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. An ambulance to a stroke-ready hospital has been arranged from the KK.
Which action should be avoided before transfer?
o: Recording the exact time that the symptoms began
Keeping her nil by mouth until a swallow screen
Giving aspirin 300 mg orally to limit the infarct
Monitoring her BP, pulse and SpO2 during the wait
Informing the receiving hospital of her arrival
mcq.e: Ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage cannot be told apart clinically, so **aspirin is withheld until CT excludes haemorrhage**; it may also complicate thrombolysis decisions. Pre-hospital care on the slides is: identify (BE-FAST, onset time), assess ABC and glucose, monitor, and transfer urgently. Keep her nil by mouth because dysphagia risks aspiration.
w: Wrong - the onset time is essential for thrombolysis decisions.
Wrong - nil by mouth is correct because dysphagia risks aspiration.
Correct - aspirin before CT could worsen an undiagnosed haemorrhage.
Wrong - monitoring vital signs is part of initial assessment.
Wrong - pre-alerting the hospital shortens door-to-needle time.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man in a KK has had sudden right hemiparesis and aphasia for 50 minutes. BP 192/104 mmHg, HR 84/min regular, glucose 7.1 mmol/L. He is alert and protecting his airway.
What is the most appropriate approach to his blood pressure?
o: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg to bring the BP below 160/90 mmHg
Oral amlodipine 10 mg stat, then recheck the BP in 30 minutes
Oral captopril 25 mg stat, aiming for a BP of 140/90 mmHg
No acute lowering in the KK; monitor and transfer urgently
IV labetalol infusion in the KK to below 140/90 mmHg
mcq.e: In acute stroke a raised BP often maintains perfusion of the ischaemic **penumbra**; **aggressive lowering in primary care can extend the infarct**. In hospital, BP is lowered only if very high (above 220/120 mmHg) or to below 185/110 mmHg if thrombolysis is planned. Sublingual nifedipine is especially dangerous because the fall is abrupt and unpredictable.
w: Wrong - sublingual nifedipine causes abrupt, uncontrolled falls in BP.
Wrong - starting antihypertensives now can reduce penumbral perfusion.
Wrong - a target of 140/90 mmHg in the first hours risks extending the infarct.
Correct - avoid acute lowering in the KK and transfer urgently.
Wrong - IV labetalol to normal values is not a KK task and the target is too low.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman went to bed at 11 pm last night feeling well. Her daughter found her at 6 am unable to move her left arm, and she was brought to the KK at 7 am.
Which time should be documented as the onset of symptoms?
o: 11 pm, when she was last known to be well
6 am, when the weakness was first discovered
7 am, when she arrived at the KK for review
3 am, the midpoint between sleep and waking
When the medical officer first examined her
mcq.e: When onset is not witnessed, the **onset time is the time last known well** - here 11 pm. Thrombolysis eligibility (within 4.5 hours) is counted from this time, so recording the discovery time could lead to unsafe thrombolysis. Wake-up strokes may still be candidates for imaging-selected treatment, so she is still referred urgently.
w: Correct - unwitnessed onset is timed from when she was last known well.
Wrong - discovery time underestimates how long the stroke has been present.
Wrong - arrival time is irrelevant to the stroke onset.
Wrong - there is no rule to take the midpoint; this is guesswork.
Wrong - the time of medical review has nothing to do with stroke onset.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man in a KK has had sudden aphasia and right arm weakness for 90 minutes. His family want to take him home first to collect his belongings and bring him to hospital in the evening.
Which counselling point about time-critical treatment is accurate?
o: IV thrombolysis can be given up to 12 hours, so the delay is fine
IV thrombolysis can be given up to 24 hours if the CT is normal
IV thrombolysis works only within 1 hour, so it is already too late
Timing does not matter because the brain damage is already fixed
IV thrombolysis must start within 4.5 hours of onset, so go now
mcq.e: **IV thrombolysis** (alteplase or tenecteplase) is given **within 4.5 hours of symptom onset**; 'time is brain' because neurons are lost every minute. **Endovascular thrombectomy** for large vessel occlusion of the MCA or ICA extends to 6-24 hours in selected patients, but only after hospital imaging, so the family should not delay.
w: Wrong - 12 hours is well beyond the thrombolysis window.
Wrong - up to 24 hours applies to selected thrombectomy, not IV thrombolysis.
Wrong - the window is 4.5 hours, so he is still eligible.
Wrong - the penumbra is salvageable, which is why speed matters.
Correct - IV thrombolysis must be started within 4.5 hours of onset.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man referred from a KK with sudden left hemiparesis for 2 hours reaches a stroke-ready hospital. The receiving doctor plans the first investigation.
Which test is the most important first step in deciding on thrombolysis?
o: MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
Carotid artery Doppler ultrasound scan
Urgent non-contrast CT scan of the brain
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain
Transthoracic echocardiogram for thrombus
mcq.e: **Urgent non-contrast CT brain** is the key acute test because it quickly excludes **haemorrhage**, which rules out thrombolysis; early ischaemic stroke may look normal. Carotid Doppler and echocardiography are post-stabilisation tests to find the cause. MRI is more sensitive but slower and less available.
w: Wrong - MRI is sensitive but slower and not the standard first test.
Wrong - carotid Doppler is a post-stabilisation test for the cause.
Correct - non-contrast CT quickly excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis.
Wrong - contrast is not needed to exclude haemorrhage and may obscure blood.
Wrong - echocardiography looks for a cardiac source later, not acutely.

mcq.stem:
A 70-kg man with acute ischaemic stroke reaches a stroke-ready hospital 2 hours after onset. CT brain excludes haemorrhage and he is eligible for IV alteplase.
What is the correct alteplase regimen?
o: Total 63 mg: 31.5 mg bolus, then 31.5 mg infused over 30 minutes
Total 63 mg: 6.3 mg bolus, then 56.7 mg infused over 60 minutes
Total 70 mg: 7 mg bolus, then 63 mg infused over 60 minutes
Total 17.5 mg given as a single IV bolus over 5 seconds
Total 90 mg: 9 mg bolus, then 81 mg infused over 60 minutes
mcq.e: Alteplase is **0.9 mg/kg** (maximum 90 mg), with **10% as a bolus** and the remaining 90% **infused over 1 hour**. For 70 kg: 63 mg total, 6.3 mg bolus and 56.7 mg over 60 minutes. A single bolus of 0.25 mg/kg (17.5 mg here) is the **tenecteplase** regimen.
w: Wrong - the bolus is 10%, not half, and the infusion runs over 60 minutes.
Correct - 0.9 mg/kg = 63 mg; 10% bolus then the rest over 1 hour.
Wrong - this uses 1 mg/kg, which overdoses him.
Wrong - a single 0.25 mg/kg bolus is tenecteplase, not alteplase.
Wrong - 90 mg is the maximum dose, for patients of 100 kg or more.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old woman is seen at a KK with sudden right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. Her pulse is 108/min and irregularly irregular. She has hypertension and has never taken an anticoagulant.
What is the most likely mechanism of her stroke?
o: Lacunar infarct from small vessel lipohyalinosis
Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage in the putamen
Paradoxical embolus through a patent foramen ovale
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis from dehydration
Cardioembolism from a left atrial appendage thrombus
mcq.e: An **irregularly irregular pulse** suggests **atrial fibrillation**, which forms thrombus in the left atrial appendage and causes **cardioembolic stroke**; cortical signs such as aphasia fit a large territory embolus rather than a lacune. The slides stress the cardiac examination (pulse, murmur, carotid bruit) and post-stabilisation ECG and echo to find the cause. CT is still needed because haemorrhage cannot be excluded clinically.
w: Wrong - lacunar strokes do not cause cortical signs such as aphasia.
Wrong - haemorrhage is possible, but AF makes embolism the most likely mechanism.
Wrong - paradoxical embolism is a cause in young patients without AF.
Wrong - venous sinus thrombosis gives headache, seizures and papilloedema.
Correct - AF with cortical signs points to cardioembolism.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old hypertensive smoker presents to a KK with 1 hour of sudden severe vertigo, double vision and slurred speech. He cannot walk without falling to the left. His face is symmetrical and arm strength is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Posterior circulation ischaemic stroke
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, posterior canal
Acute vestibular neuritis
Ménière disease attack
Acute labyrinthitis
mcq.e: FAST misses **posterior circulation** strokes, which present with **vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia** - hence **BE-FAST** adds Balance and Eyes. Peripheral vestibular disorders do not cause diplopia, dysarthria or inability to stand, and BPPV is brief and positional. He needs urgent transfer within the thrombolysis window.
w: Correct - vertigo with diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia is central until proven otherwise.
Wrong - BPPV gives brief positional vertigo without diplopia or dysarthria.
Wrong - vestibular neuritis causes vertigo but no diplopia or dysarthria.
Wrong - Ménière disease causes vertigo with tinnitus and hearing loss, not brainstem signs.
Wrong - labyrinthitis adds hearing loss but no brainstem signs.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old man attends a KK after 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech that started this morning and fully resolved before arrival. Examination is now normal, capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L and there was no headache or jerking.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Minor ischaemic stroke
Todd paresis after a seizure
Migraine with motor aura
Transient ischaemic attack
Hypoglycaemic episode
mcq.e: The slides define stroke as a focal deficit lasting **more than 24 hours**; a deficit that **resolves completely within 24 hours** (usually within minutes) is a **transient ischaemic attack**. TIA carries a high early stroke risk, so it needs urgent same-day assessment and secondary prevention, not reassurance. Normal glucose and no seizure make the mimics unlikely.
w: Wrong - a stroke has deficits lasting over 24 hours; his resolved within 20 minutes.
Wrong - Todd paresis follows a seizure, and there was no jerking.
Wrong - migraine aura spreads gradually and is usually followed by headache.
Correct - focal deficit resolving fully within 24 hours is a TIA.
Wrong - his glucose is normal.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old rubber tapper is brought to a KK 2 hours after being bitten on the hand by a snake that reared up and spread a hood. He is anxious but talking normally, with local pain and swelling.
Which sign is the earliest and most reliable indicator of neurotoxic envenoming?
o: Paradoxical abdominal breathing
Inability to lift the head off the bed
Ptosis of both upper eyelids
Pooled secretions and nasal voice
Dilated pupils with diplopia
mcq.e: Elapid (cobra, krait, sea snake) neurotoxins cause **descending flaccid paralysis**, and **ptosis is the earliest and most reliable sign**, followed by ophthalmoplegia, bulbar palsy, neck flexor weakness ('broken neck sign') and finally respiratory paralysis. Spotting ptosis early allows antivenom and airway support to be arranged before respiratory failure.
w: Wrong - paradoxical breathing is a late sign of respiratory muscle paralysis.
Wrong - the broken neck sign appears after cranial nerve involvement.
Correct - ptosis is the earliest and most reliable sign of neurotoxicity.
Wrong - bulbar palsy follows the earlier ocular signs.
Wrong - pupil and ocular muscle signs occur, but ptosis is the earliest reliable sign.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old plantation worker in northern Peninsular Malaysia is bitten on the ankle at dusk by a brown snake with dark triangular markings lying in leaf litter. Six hours later the leg is swollen to the knee with blisters, her gums are oozing and the venepuncture site keeps bleeding. There is no ptosis.
Which snake is the most likely culprit?
o: Malayan krait (Bungarus candidus)
Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma)
Monocled cobra (Naja kaouthia)
Beaked sea snake (Hydrophis schistosus)
Red-necked keelback (Rhabdophis subminiatus)
mcq.e: **Viperid** venom is **haematotoxic** and cytotoxic: progressive swelling, blistering and **spontaneous bleeding** from gums and puncture sites from venom-induced consumption coagulopathy. The **Malayan pit viper** is the classic culprit in northern Peninsular Malaysia. The red-necked keelback can cause coagulopathy but rarely marked local tissue damage; kraits and sea snakes cause neurotoxicity or myotoxicity with little local swelling.
w: Wrong - krait bites cause neurotoxicity with minimal local swelling.
Correct - marked local swelling, blistering and bleeding point to the Malayan pit viper.
Wrong - cobras cause local necrosis and neurotoxicity, not spontaneous bleeding.
Wrong - sea snakes bite in the sea and cause myotoxicity.
Wrong - the keelback can cause coagulopathy but not this degree of local damage; it is rare.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old fisherman from Kuala Kedah is bitten on the hand while pulling in a net. The bite was painless and he has only faint puncture marks. Three hours later he complains of generalised muscle aches, jaw stiffness and pain when his thighs are squeezed. He passed dark brown urine at the Klinik Kesihatan. BP 128/78 mmHg, no ptosis, no bleeding.
Which serial blood test, repeated every 4-6 hours, best tracks the main venom effect in this patient?
o: Creatine kinase
Prothrombin time and INR
Serum fibrinogen
Serum lipase
Cardiac troponin
mcq.e: Painless bite at sea followed by **myalgia, trismus, muscle tenderness and myoglobinuria** is **sea snake myotoxicity** (rhabdomyolysis). The MOH guideline recommends **serial CK every 4-6 hours**, plus renal profile and **potassium** because hyperkalaemia and oliguric AKI are the killers. Coagulation tests are the serial tests for pit viper and unidentified bites, not sea snakes.
w: Correct - CK every 4-6 hours detects and tracks rhabdomyolysis from sea snake myotoxins.
Wrong - PT/INR 6-hourly is for pit viper and unidentified bites; sea snake venom is not mainly haematotoxic.
Wrong - fibrinogen is sent only when coagulopathy is present; there is no bleeding here.
Wrong - lipase has no role; the brown urine is myoglobin, not a pancreatic problem.
Wrong - troponin does not track skeletal muscle breakdown; ECG is used to watch for hyperkalaemia.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old rubber tapper walks into a Klinik Kesihatan in Pahang 20 minutes after being bitten on the left forearm by a snake he did not see clearly. There are two puncture marks with mild local pain. He is anxious; BP 132/84 mmHg, pulse 98/min, no ptosis and no bleeding. The ambulance has been called.
Which first-aid measure is most appropriate while awaiting transfer?
o: Tie a tight band just above the elbow to stop venom spread
Make a small incision over the fang marks and suck out venom
Apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth over the bite site
Keep him still and splint the forearm at heart level
Give IM promethazine to prevent a reaction to antivenom
mcq.e: MOH first aid is **reassure, keep the patient still, and immobilise the limb** with a splint or sling in a neutral position at heart level, then refer urgently because the bite is **unidentified**. Tourniquets cause ischaemia and a surge of venom on release; incision, suction and ice damage tissue and do not remove venom. **IM injections are avoided** in case this is a pit viper bite with coagulopathy.
w: Wrong - tourniquets cause limb ischaemia and a bolus of venom when released; they are harmful.
Wrong - incision and suction remove no useful venom and add bleeding and infection.
Wrong - ice worsens local tissue damage and does not slow systemic absorption.
Correct - rest and splinting at heart level slow lymphatic spread of venom.
Wrong - IM injections are avoided in possible viper bites, and premedication is not a first-aid step.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old woman is under observation at a district hospital after a pit viper bite on the right ankle 4 hours ago. The swelling now reaches mid-calf. The medical officer wants to know whether the swelling is advancing quickly enough to influence the decision on antivenom.
Which method of monitoring is recommended?
o: Measure calf circumference with a tape measure every hour
Tape the advancing edge every 2-3 hours and calculate cm/hour
Draw a line at the swelling edge with a permanent marker every 6 hours
Request a Doppler ultrasound of the calf every 12 hours
Photograph the limb every 6 hours and compare the images
mcq.e: The MOH guideline measures the **rate of proximal progression (RPP)**: removable **micropore tape** strips mark the advancing margin at fixed intervals (every **2-3 hours**) so the speed in cm/hour can be calculated. **Limb girth is not recommended** because venom swelling moves proximally rather than building up at one level. Permanent markers are discouraged because they cannot be repositioned and stain the skin.
w: Wrong - girth at a fixed point misses venom swelling that travels proximally.
Correct - micropore tape at the advancing edge every 2-3 hours gives the rate of proximal progression.
Wrong - permanent markers are specifically discouraged, and 6-hourly is too infrequent.
Wrong - Doppler looks for DVT; it does not quantify envenoming swelling.
Wrong - photographs are imprecise and do not give a rate in cm/hour.

mcq.stem:
A 36-year-old man bitten by a Malayan pit viper 6 hours ago has oozing from the bite site and gums. His INR is 3.4 and platelets 62 x10^9/L. He is drowsy after vomiting repeatedly, and the doctor wants to assess his acid-base status.
Which procedure should be avoided in this patient?
o: Peripheral venous cannulation in the forearm
Repeat 20-minute whole blood clotting test
Urine FEME for haematuria
Twelve-lead ECG
Radial artery puncture for blood gas
mcq.e: With **viper coagulopathy**, **arterial puncture is strictly contraindicated** because an arterial bleed cannot be compressed easily and may form an uncontrollable haematoma. A **venous blood gas** answers the acid-base question. Peripheral IV access, serial clotting tests, urinalysis and ECG are all part of routine monitoring; **IM injections** should also be avoided.
w: Wrong - peripheral IV access is needed for fluids and antivenom and can be compressed.
Wrong - serial 20WBCT is how response to antivenom is monitored.
Wrong - urinalysis screens for haematuria and is non-invasive.
Wrong - ECG is safe and part of baseline monitoring.
Correct - arterial puncture in viper coagulopathy risks an uncontrollable haematoma.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old man brings a dead snake in a plastic bag to a Klinik Kesihatan, 1 hour after it bit his calf while he was clearing a drain. He has two shallow scratches with no bleeding, swelling or systemic symptoms. He wants to go home.
Which condition must be met before he can safely be discharged?
o: He has had no swelling after 1 hour of observation
A single 20-minute whole blood clotting test is normal
A trained expert identifies the snake as a non-venomous species
He is given tetanus toxoid and a course of oral antibiotics
The snake is less than 50 cm long, so the venom load is small
mcq.e: The MOH guideline allows discharge only if **the snake is positively identified as non-venomous by a trained expert**, the clinical picture fits that species, and there is no significant tissue injury. Otherwise the bite is treated as **venomous or unidentified** and the patient is admitted for observation. Envenoming can be delayed for hours (especially kraits), so one normal test or a short quiet period is not enough, and small or juvenile snakes can still envenom.
w: Wrong - envenoming may be delayed for many hours, so 1 hour of observation is not reassuring.
Wrong - one early normal clotting test does not exclude later coagulopathy or neurotoxicity.
Correct - expert identification as non-venomous is the first discharge criterion.
Wrong - wound care may be needed but does not make the patient safe to go home.
Wrong - juvenile snakes can deliver dangerous venom; size does not decide safety.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old farmer from Perlis is referred from the Klinik Kesihatan to the district hospital emergency department 3 hours after a snake bite on the foot. The snake was not seen. The foot is swollen and tender. Blood placed in a clean, dry glass tube and left undisturbed for 20 minutes is still liquid when the tube is tipped.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give antivenom now and repeat the clotting test 6 hours later
Transfuse fresh frozen plasma first and give antivenom only if bleeding starts
Give IM vitamin K and repeat the clotting test in 6 hours
Observe and give antivenom only if the next test 6 hours later is also abnormal
Start IV heparin to stop the consumption coagulopathy
mcq.e: Unclotted blood at 20 minutes means **venom-induced consumption coagulopathy**, a definite **indication for antivenom** (chosen by species or by the syndromic approach for unidentified bites). The 20WBCT is repeated about **6 hours** after antivenom to judge whether more is needed. FFP does not neutralise venom, vitamin K does not correct it, delaying treatment risks serious bleeding, and heparin is harmful.
w: Correct - an abnormal 20WBCT indicates systemic envenoming that needs antivenom without delay.
Wrong - FFP is consumed by circulating venom; antivenom is the definitive treatment and should not wait for bleeding.
Wrong - this coagulopathy is not vitamin K deficiency; vitamin K does not reverse it.
Wrong - a confirmed coagulopathy is already an indication; waiting risks haemorrhage.
Wrong - heparin does not stop venom-induced consumption and increases bleeding.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old boy sleeping on the floor of a kampung house woke at 3 am with abdominal pain after feeling something on his arm. By 8 am at the Klinik Kesihatan he has bilateral ptosis, a nasal voice, pooled saliva in his mouth, and cannot lift his head from the pillow. His abdomen moves inwards as his chest rises. SpO2 93% on room air.
What is the most immediate priority?
o: Give the first vial of antivenom before attending to the airway
Perform a 20-minute whole blood clotting test to confirm the snake type
Suction, position the airway and support breathing with bag-valve-mask
Give nebulised salbutamol for the respiratory difficulty
Wait for the 6-hourly neurological chart to show progression
mcq.e: Night bite while asleep on the floor with little local reaction suggests a **krait**. Bulbar palsy, the **broken neck sign** and **paradoxical abdominal breathing** mean impending **respiratory failure**, so airway and breathing come first: suction secretions, position, oxygen and **assisted ventilation**, with urgent transfer for intubation and antivenom. Antivenom works slowly on established neurotoxicity and never replaces ventilatory support.
w: Wrong - antivenom is needed, but an obstructed airway and failing ventilation kill first.
Wrong - clotting tests do not help an imminent respiratory arrest and kraits rarely cause coagulopathy.
Correct - neurotoxic respiratory failure needs immediate airway and ventilatory support.
Wrong - this is neuromuscular weakness, not bronchospasm.
Wrong - paradoxical breathing already shows severe paralysis; delay can cause arrest.

mcq.stem:
A mother brings her 7-year-old son to a Klinik Kesihatan in Kelantan 40 minutes after he stepped on something in long grass at dusk and cried out. Nobody saw the animal. There are two small puncture marks on the dorsum of the foot. He is well, with no swelling, ptosis or bleeding.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure, clean the wound and discharge with advice to return if swelling appears
Observe in the clinic for 1 hour and discharge if he remains well
Give a prophylactic dose of antivenom before he leaves the clinic
Prescribe oral cloxacillin and review him in the clinic the next day
Refer to hospital for admission and observation with serial clotting tests
mcq.e: An **unidentified snake or animal bite** is itself an **indication for observation and admission** under the MOH guideline, even if the patient looks well, because envenoming can appear late. He needs hospital observation (usually at least 24 hours) with serial clotting tests and neurological checks. Antivenom is never given prophylactically.
w: Wrong - an unidentified bite must not be discharged home from primary care.
Wrong - 1 hour is far too short; delayed envenoming is well recognised.
Wrong - antivenom is given only for signs of envenoming because of anaphylaxis risk and cost.
Wrong - antibiotics are not the issue; the risk is unrecognised envenoming.
Correct - unidentified bites need hospital observation with serial monitoring.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old oil palm worker in Johor disturbed a snake that raised its front body, spread a flat hood and spat towards his face before biting his hand. Four hours later the hand is painfully swollen with blisters and a dusky purple patch. He also has drooping eyelids. Clotting test is normal.
Which snake is most likely responsible?
o: Malayan pit viper
Banded krait
Red-necked keelback
Spitting cobra
Beaked sea snake
mcq.e: **Hooding and spitting** are cobra behaviours. Cobras (Naja) are elapids whose venom is both **cytotoxic** (painful swelling, blistering, dermonecrosis) and **neurotoxic** (ptosis). Pit vipers cause local damage plus **coagulopathy**; kraits cause neurotoxicity with **minimal local signs**; the red-necked keelback causes coagulopathy; sea snakes cause myotoxicity.
w: Wrong - pit vipers cause coagulopathy and do not hood, spit or cause ptosis.
Wrong - kraits cause neurotoxicity with little or no local swelling or necrosis.
Wrong - the keelback is the one keelback that causes coagulopathy, not necrosis with ptosis.
Correct - hooding, spitting, local necrosis and ptosis point to a cobra.
Wrong - sea snakes bite in the sea and cause rhabdomyolysis.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old girl in Kuching, Sarawak, is bitten on the hand by a stray dog that ran off. There are two puncture wounds that bled. She has never received rabies vaccine. The wound has been washed with soap and running water for 15 minutes.
Which post-exposure prophylaxis is indicated?
o: Rabies vaccine course alone, without immunoglobulin
Rabies vaccine course plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wounds
Rabies immunoglobulin alone, without a vaccine course
No prophylaxis unless the dog shows signs of rabies within 14 days
A single booster dose of rabies vaccine only
mcq.e: Transdermal bites that bleed in a **rabies-infected area** (Sarawak) are **WHO category III**: wound washing, a full **vaccine course** and **rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)** infiltrated into and around the wounds. RIG gives immediate passive cover until vaccine antibodies appear. PEP is never delayed waiting for a missing stray to show signs, and a booster-only schedule is for people already fully vaccinated.
w: Wrong - vaccine alone is for category II exposures such as minor scratches without bleeding.
Correct - category III needs vaccine plus RIG infiltrated into the wounds.
Wrong - RIG without vaccine gives only short passive protection.
Wrong - the dog is a stray that has gone, and PEP must not wait in an infected area.
Wrong - booster doses without RIG apply only to previously vaccinated people.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man in Sibu, Sarawak, attends a Klinik Kesihatan after a free-roaming dog nipped his bare forearm. Examination shows a superficial abrasion with no bleeding and no puncture wound. He has never had rabies vaccine. The wound has been washed for 15 minutes.
What is the most appropriate post-exposure management?
o: Wound care and tetanus cover only, since the skin was not punctured
Rabies immunoglobulin into the abrasion plus a full vaccine course
Rabies immunoglobulin into the abrasion without vaccine
A full rabies vaccine course without immunoglobulin
Defer prophylaxis while the dog is traced and observed for 14 days
mcq.e: Nibbling of bare skin or **minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding** are **WHO category II**: wash the wound and start the **rabies vaccine course**; RIG is not needed. Bleeding bites, scratches that bleed, licks on broken skin and mucosal contact are category III and need RIG as well. In an infected area such as Sarawak, PEP starts at once and may be stopped only if a traced animal stays healthy through observation or tests negative.
w: Wrong - an abrasion of bare skin is a category II exposure, not category I.
Wrong - RIG is reserved for category III exposures such as bleeding bites.
Wrong - RIG alone never gives lasting protection.
Correct - category II needs wound washing plus vaccine without RIG.
Wrong - PEP must not be delayed in a rabies-infected area while a free-roaming dog is traced.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man arrives at a Klinik Kesihatan 30 minutes after his neighbour’s dog bit his calf, leaving several puncture wounds and a 2 cm ragged laceration. He is haemodynamically stable and bleeding has stopped with pressure.
What is the single most important first step in his wound management?
o: Flush and scrub the wounds with soap and running water for 15 minutes
Close the laceration with sutures to reduce later scarring
Apply antibiotic ointment and a dry occlusive dressing
Start oral amoxicillin-clavulanate before cleaning the wound
Give tetanus toxoid first, then dress the wound
mcq.e: The MOH rabies guideline calls **thorough washing with soap or detergent and running water for at least 15 minutes** the single most critical step: it physically removes and inactivates virus and bacteria. Povidone-iodine or 70% alcohol is applied afterwards. Primary **suturing is avoided** because it may drive virus deeper; antibiotics and tetanus cover are adjuncts after cleaning, not replacements.
w: Correct - prolonged washing with soap and running water is the most effective early measure.
Wrong - suturing bite wounds is avoided because it may inoculate virus deeper and trap bacteria.
Wrong - ointment and occlusion without washing leave virus and bacteria in the wound.
Wrong - antibiotics are an adjunct for deep or contaminated wounds and come after cleaning.
Wrong - tetanus cover is needed, but wound washing is the priority step.

mcq.stem:
A medical officer at a Klinik Kesihatan in Perak has just finished washing a category III dog bite on a 12-year-old boy and arranged his hospital referral for rabies prophylaxis. The dog belongs to a neighbour and is still alive.
Which notification step is required?
o: Notify the police within 7 days so that the dog owner can be charged with negligence
Notify only if the boy later develops symptoms suggestive of rabies
Notify the State Health Department within 1 week by telephone
No notification is needed because the dog has an identifiable owner
Complete the Animal Bite Notification Form to the DHO and DVO within 24 hours
mcq.e: Every animal bite is notified using the **Animal Bite Notification Form within 24 hours** to the **District Health Office and District Veterinary Office**. This lets the veterinary team trace, observe or test the animal and lets public health find other exposed people. Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose, because rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear.
w: Wrong - the purpose is disease control through health and veterinary offices, not prosecution.
Wrong - notification is for every bite; symptomatic rabies is too late to prevent.
Wrong - the deadline is 24 hours, to the district health and veterinary offices.
Wrong - owned dogs still need tracing, observation and vaccination checks.
Correct - the bite notification form goes to the DHO and DVO within 24 hours.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man from Serian, Sarawak, presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of fever, headache and tingling around a healed wound on his left hand, from a dog bite 7 weeks ago that he did not report. Today he is agitated, and when offered a cup of water his neck and throat muscles go into painful spasm. He also flinches when a fan blows on his face.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Generalised tetanus
Japanese encephalitis
Encephalitic rabies
Acute dystonic reaction
Guillain-Barré syndrome
mcq.e: A prodrome of **fever with paraesthesia at the old bite site**, then agitation with **hydrophobia** (pharyngeal spasm triggered by trying to drink) and **aerophobia** (spasm from a draught), is classic **encephalitic (furious) rabies**. Tetanus causes trismus, risus sardonicus and spasms set off by touch or noise, but not spasms specific to water or air. Once symptoms appear rabies is almost always fatal, which is why prompt PEP matters.
w: Wrong - tetanus causes trismus and generalised spasms, not hydrophobia or aerophobia.
Wrong - Japanese encephalitis causes fever and altered consciousness without hydrophobia or bite-site paraesthesia.
Correct - bite-site paraesthesia, hydrophobia and aerophobia after a dog bite in Sarawak mean rabies.
Wrong - dystonic reactions follow dopamine blockers and are not triggered by water or air.
Wrong - GBS is ascending weakness without agitation, hydrophobia or fever.

mcq.stem:
A mother brings her 6-year-old son to a Klinik Kesihatan in Sarawak 2 hours after a stray dog bit him on the face, causing two bleeding puncture wounds. The dog was caught by neighbours. She asks for a blood test to find out whether her son has caught rabies before agreeing to injections.
What is the most appropriate response?
o: Send serum for rabies neutralising antibodies and decide on PEP when results return
Explain that no test detects rabies before symptoms, so PEP is decided on the exposure
Send saliva for rabies rRT-PCR and start PEP only if positive
Arrange a nuchal skin biopsy to look for rabies antigen first
Wait for the dog’s brain fluorescent antibody result before starting any vaccine
mcq.e: **No test can detect human rabies during the incubation period**; nuchal skin biopsy, saliva, CSF and urine rRT-PCR are only for patients who already have symptoms. The decision is based on the **exposure category and animal risk**: a bleeding facial bite in Sarawak is category III and needs immediate wound care, vaccine and RIG. PEP is started straight away and can be stopped if the dog’s brain DFA test is negative.
w: Wrong - antibodies are absent in incubation; waiting wastes critical time with a facial bite.
Correct - human tests cannot detect incubating rabies, so the exposure risk decides PEP.
Wrong - saliva PCR is used only for symptomatic patients and is negative during incubation.
Wrong - nuchal biopsy is an ante-mortem test for symptomatic patients only.
Wrong - PEP must not be delayed for the animal result, especially for a facial bite.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan 3 hours after her pet cat bit her right index finger, leaving two deep puncture wounds. She has no drug allergies, is fully immunised against tetanus and the wound has been irrigated.
Which oral antibiotic is the most appropriate prophylaxis?
o: Cloxacillin for 5 days
Cephalexin for 5 days
Erythromycin for 5 days
Metronidazole for 5 days
Co-amoxiclav for 5 days
mcq.e: Deep cat bites, especially on the **hand**, carry a high risk of **Pasteurella multocida** infection, which can appear within hours and spread to tendon sheaths and joints. **Amoxicillin-clavulanate** covers Pasteurella, staphylococci, streptococci and anaerobes. The trap is cloxacillin or cephalexin: they cover skin flora but **miss Pasteurella**; erythromycin is unreliable and metronidazole covers only anaerobes.
w: Wrong - cloxacillin covers staphylococci but not Pasteurella multocida.
Wrong - first-generation cephalosporins have poor activity against Pasteurella.
Wrong - erythromycin is unreliable against Pasteurella.
Wrong - metronidazole covers anaerobes only.
Correct - co-amoxiclav covers Pasteurella and mixed oral flora after a cat bite.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old girl is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with a tender, 3 cm swelling in her right axilla for 2 weeks. She is otherwise well, with a low-grade fever. Her family adopted a kitten 5 weeks ago, and there is a small healing papule on her right forearm where it scratched her. There is no weight loss or night sweats.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Bartonella henselae
Pasteurella multocida
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Toxoplasma gondii
Sporothrix schenckii
mcq.e: A primary inoculation papule followed weeks later by **tender regional lymphadenopathy** in a child who handles a kitten is **cat scratch disease** (Bartonella henselae), which is also spread by cat fleas. Its onset is **slower** than Pasteurella, which causes cellulitis within hours. Most cases are **benign and self-limiting**; warm compresses help, and persistent nodes may need a macrolide. Note: slide p52 gives erythromycin for 10 days; current practice usually uses azithromycin for 5 days.
w: Correct - scratch papule plus tender regional nodes weeks later is cat scratch disease.
Wrong - Pasteurella causes rapid cellulitis within hours, not node enlargement weeks later.
Wrong - TB nodes are usually painless and come with constitutional symptoms.
Wrong - toxoplasmosis gives generalised, often non-tender nodes without an inoculation papule.
Wrong - sporotrichosis causes nodules along lymphatics after plant or soil injury.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old tourist is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan on Pulau Langkawi after a jellyfish brushed her leg while swimming. She has intense burning pain and linear red raised streaks on the calf. Tentacle fragments have been removed. Vital signs are normal and she has no breathing difficulty, chest pain or vomiting.
Which measure gives the best pain relief?
o: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel for 20 minutes at a time
Apply a pressure immobilisation bandage over the leg
Hot water immersion at 40-45 °C for up to 90 minutes
Apply hydrocortisone cream and give an oral antihistamine
Give IM promethazine and observe for 1 hour
mcq.e: **Hot water immersion at 40-45 °C** (bath or shower, for up to **90 minutes**) is thought to inactivate heat-labile venom and gives **better pain relief** than vinegar, papain or opioids in trials. Test the temperature on unaffected skin first to avoid scalds. Pressure bandaging is no longer advised for jellyfish stings, and antihistamines or steroid cream help itch but not the acute venom pain.
w: Wrong - cold packs give less pain relief than hot water immersion.
Wrong - pressure bandages may squeeze more venom from undischarged nematocysts.
Correct - hot water at 40-45 °C for up to 90 minutes gives the best pain relief.
Wrong - these help itch and inflammation later but do little for the acute pain.
Wrong - she has no allergic reaction; sedating antihistamines do not treat venom pain.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old diver in Sabah feels a mild sting on his forearm with little to see on the skin. Forty minutes later he develops severe lower back pain, generalised muscle cramps, profuse sweating, restlessness and a sense of impending doom. BP 190/110 mmHg, pulse 128/min, no urticaria or wheeze.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Anaphylaxis to jellyfish venom
Acute coronary syndrome
Panic attack after the sting
Irukandji syndrome
Acute renal colic
