mcq.e: A **minor-looking sting** followed 20-40 minutes later by severe back and muscle pain, sweating, agitation, **hypertension and tachycardia** is **Irukandji syndrome** (Carukia barnesi and related small box jellyfish). It reflects a catecholamine surge and can cause heart failure, cardiac arrest and death, so it needs urgent transfer, analgesia and BP control. Anaphylaxis would cause **hypotension**, urticaria or wheeze, not marked hypertension.
w: Wrong - anaphylaxis causes hypotension, urticaria or bronchospasm rather than hypertension and cramps.
Wrong - ACS does not explain the sting, the cramps and the generalised muscle pain.
Wrong - this is a dangerous envenoming syndrome; calling it panic delays life-saving care.
Correct - delayed back pain, cramps, sweating, hypertension and tachycardia after a minor sting mean Irukandji syndrome.
Wrong - renal colic does not cause generalised cramps and sweating after a sting.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy is carried out of the sea at a beach in Terengganu screaming, with long tentacles still stuck across his thighs. A lifeguard suspects a box jellyfish. The boy is breathing normally with a palpable pulse. Household vinegar, a bottle of mineral water and a towel are available.
Before removing the tentacles, what should be poured over them?
o: Mineral water, to wash the venom away
Household vinegar, for at least 30 seconds
Alcohol-based hand sanitiser
Cold water, followed by rubbing with the towel
Fresh human urine
mcq.e: For **box jellyfish**, dousing with **4-5% acetic acid (household vinegar)** for at least 30 seconds inactivates the **undischarged nematocysts** so that more venom is not fired while tentacles are lifted off. Fresh water, alcohol, urine and rubbing all make nematocysts discharge. Note: slide p56 lists vinegar under analgesia; its main role is to stop further envenoming, while hot water gives the pain relief.
w: Wrong - fresh water triggers nematocysts to fire through an osmotic change.
Correct - vinegar inactivates undischarged box jellyfish nematocysts before tentacle removal.
Wrong - alcohol can trigger nematocyst discharge.
Wrong - fresh water and rubbing both fire more nematocysts.
Wrong - urine is a myth and may trigger more discharge.

mcq.stem:
A 15-year-old girl is stung on the forearm by a jellyfish at Port Dickson and walks to the beachside first-aid post. She has burning pain and red linear weals. A few tentacle fragments are still stuck to the skin. Breathing and pulse are normal. A new volunteer starts to help.
Which action should the volunteer avoid?
o: Lifting off the remaining tentacles with tweezers or gloved fingers
Rinsing the area with seawater to wash off loose fragments
Immersing the forearm in hot water at about 42 °C
Giving oral paracetamol for the pain
Rinsing the area with fresh tap water from a bottle
mcq.e: Venom is delivered by **nematocysts**, which fire on contact. **Fresh water** changes the osmotic balance and makes undischarged nematocysts fire, so it worsens envenoming; rubbing, sand, alcohol and urine do the same. Seawater rinsing, removing tentacles with gloves or tweezers, hot water immersion and simple analgesia are all appropriate.
w: Wrong - removing tentacles with protection is correct first aid.
Wrong - seawater does not trigger nematocysts and is safe for rinsing.
Wrong - hot water immersion is the recommended way to relieve pain.
Wrong - simple analgesia is appropriate for a mild sting.
Correct - fresh water makes remaining nematocysts fire and should be avoided.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man is brought into a Klinik Kesihatan 10 minutes after being stung by wasps while cutting grass. He has generalised urticaria, swollen lips, audible wheeze and feels faint. BP 78/46 mmHg, pulse 124/min, SpO2 91%. A peripheral IV line is not yet in place.
What is the first drug to give?
o: IV adrenaline 0.5 mg as a rapid bolus once a line is in
IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh
SC adrenaline 0.5 mg into the upper outer arm
IV hydrocortisone 200 mg once a line is in
IV chlorpheniramine 10 mg once a line is in
mcq.e: Urticaria and angioedema with **wheeze and hypotension** after a sting is **anaphylaxis**. The first drug is **IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000), 0.5 mg for an adult, into the anterolateral thigh**, which is absorbed faster than the subcutaneous route. Undiluted IV bolus adrenaline can cause fatal arrhythmias and is for specialists in monitored settings; steroids and antihistamines are second-line and must never delay adrenaline.
w: Wrong - IV bolus adrenaline risks arrhythmias and waiting for access delays treatment.
Correct - IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh is first-line for adult anaphylaxis.
Wrong - subcutaneous absorption is slow and unreliable, especially in shock.
Wrong - steroids act over hours and do not reverse shock or airway swelling.
Wrong - antihistamines only help skin symptoms and do not treat shock or bronchospasm.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy weighing 25 kg is stung by a bee at school and develops facial swelling, hoarse voice, wheeze and vomiting within 15 minutes. At the Klinik Kesihatan he is pale with BP 70/40 mmHg. The nurse has a 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline ampoule and a 1 mL syringe ready.
What is the correct dose to give?
o: 0.25 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) adrenaline IM
2.5 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline IM
0.05 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline IM
0.25 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline IM
0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline IM
mcq.e: The paediatric dose is **0.01 mg/kg IM, maximum 0.5 mg**: 25 kg x 0.01 = **0.25 mg**, which is **0.25 mL of 1 mg/mL** adrenaline, into the anterolateral thigh. Using 1:10,000 at the same volume gives a tenth of the dose, and 2.5 mL of 1:1000 is a tenfold overdose. The 0.5 mL dose is the adult maximum, double what this child needs.
w: Wrong - 0.25 mL of 1:10,000 is only 0.025 mg, one tenth of the required dose.
Wrong - 2.5 mL of 1:1000 is 2.5 mg, a dangerous tenfold overdose.
Wrong - 0.05 mg is far too little for a 25 kg child.
Correct - 0.01 mg/kg x 25 kg = 0.25 mg = 0.25 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline.
Wrong - 0.5 mg is the adult maximum and twice this child’s weight-based dose.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman with anaphylaxis after a bee sting received IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the thigh at the Klinik Kesihatan 5 minutes ago. She is lying with her legs raised on high-flow oxygen, and IV saline has been started. She is still wheezy with BP 82/50 mmHg and pulse 130/min. The ambulance is 20 minutes away.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the thigh now
Give IV chlorpheniramine and reassess in 15 minutes
Wait 15 minutes for the first dose to take full effect
Give oral prednisolone 50 mg and continue IV fluids
Switch to nebulised salbutamol instead of more adrenaline
mcq.e: If shock or bronchospasm **persists 5 minutes after the first dose**, **repeat IM adrenaline** while continuing oxygen, IV crystalloid and monitoring until transfer. Waiting longer allows the reaction to progress. Salbutamol can be added for persistent bronchospasm but does not treat shock, and antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only.
w: Correct - persistent shock 5 minutes after the first dose needs repeat IM adrenaline.
Wrong - antihistamines do not reverse shock and the wait wastes time.
Wrong - the slide repeats adrenaline after 5 minutes; waiting 15 minutes is too long.
Wrong - oral steroids act over hours and she may not swallow safely.
Wrong - salbutamol is an add-on for wheeze, not a substitute for adrenaline in shock.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old gardener attends a Klinik Kesihatan the day after a wasp sting on the forearm. The redness and swelling now extend 14 cm from the sting site and have been increasing for 26 hours, with itch and mild pain. He has no fever, no lymphangitis, no urticaria elsewhere and no breathing problems. Vital signs are normal.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral cloxacillin for 7 days to treat cellulitis
IM adrenaline 0.5 mg and transfer to the emergency department
Cold compress, analgesia, antihistamine and a short steroid course
Prescribe an adrenaline autoinjector and refer for venom immunotherapy now
Incise and drain the swollen area to release venom
mcq.e: Swelling **beyond 10 cm lasting more than 24 hours** with no systemic features is a **large local reaction**, an IgE-mediated late-phase reaction rather than infection. Treat with **cold compresses, analgesia, an oral antihistamine** and consider a **short oral steroid course** for severe swelling. Antibiotics are a common mistake: infection is rare, and itch with no fever points away from cellulitis. The risk of future anaphylaxis is low, so an autoinjector and immunotherapy are not routinely needed.
w: Wrong - this is allergic inflammation, not infection; antibiotics are not indicated.
Wrong - there are no systemic features, so this is not anaphylaxis.
Correct - a large local reaction is managed with cold compress, analgesia, antihistamine and possibly a short steroid course.
Wrong - immunotherapy is for previous systemic reactions, not large local reactions.
Wrong - incision does not remove venom and adds infection risk.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old beekeeper is reviewed at a Klinik Kesihatan a week after being treated in the emergency department for anaphylaxis with hypotension and wheeze after a bee sting. He has fully recovered and plans to keep his bee farm.
Besides training him to use an adrenaline autoinjector, which step best reduces his risk of a future fatal reaction?
o: Daily oral cetirizine during the honey harvest season
A short prednisolone course before each hive inspection
Skin-prick testing at the Klinik Kesihatan to confirm the allergy
Advice to wear light-coloured clothing with no further action
Referral to an allergy or immunology service for venom immunotherapy
mcq.e: A previous **systemic** reaction to a sting is the indication for **specialist allergy/immunology referral** to assess for **venom immunotherapy**, which greatly reduces the risk of future systemic reactions. Antihistamines and steroids do not prevent anaphylaxis. Avoidance advice is useful but not enough for a beekeeper, and venom testing should be done in a specialist setting.
w: Wrong - antihistamines do not prevent venom anaphylaxis.
Wrong - steroid premedication does not reliably prevent anaphylaxis and has side effects.
Wrong - venom testing belongs in a specialist allergy setting with resuscitation ready.
Wrong - avoidance helps but cannot protect a beekeeper on its own.
Correct - venom immunotherapy after a systemic reaction greatly reduces future risk.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old woman collapses in the waiting area of a Klinik Kesihatan after a bee sting on the neck. She is conscious but drowsy, with widespread urticaria, BP 70/40 mmHg and pulse 136/min. She has no stridor and only mild breathlessness. IM adrenaline has been given. She insists on getting up to walk to the toilet.
How should she be positioned?
o: Lying flat on her back with her legs raised
Sitting upright in a chair to ease her breathing
Standing with support to walk to the ambulance
Lying prone with her head turned to one side
Propped up at 45 degrees with her legs dependent
mcq.e: In anaphylactic shock, venous pooling and capillary leak leave the heart with little preload. Sitting or standing suddenly can cause an **empty ventricle**, cardiac arrest and death. Keep her **supine with legs elevated** and move her lying down. Patients with mainly breathing difficulty may sit up, but only if they are not hypotensive.
w: Correct - supine with legs raised maintains venous return in anaphylactic shock.
Wrong - sitting up when hypotensive can precipitate cardiovascular collapse.
Wrong - standing or walking in anaphylaxis has caused sudden death.
Wrong - prone positioning hinders monitoring and does not help venous return.
Wrong - dependent legs reduce venous return and worsen shock.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks attends a Klinik Kesihatan with an alternative birthing centre in early labour. Her antenatal course has been low risk. The midwife records several observations.
Which finding requires urgent referral to hospital?
o: Blood pressure 136/86 mmHg
Oral temperature 37.4 °C
Contractions 3 in 10 minutes, each lasting 40 seconds
Fetal heart rate 104/min between contractions
Cervix 3 cm dilated with intact membranes
mcq.e: Urgent referral criteria include **abnormal fetal heart rate below 110 or above 160/min**, **BP of 140/90 or more**, fever, bleeding, meconium, cord prolapse, malpresentation, **preterm labour under 37 weeks** and abnormal progress. A baseline of 104/min is fetal bradycardia and suggests fetal compromise. The other findings are within normal limits for early labour.
w: Wrong - 136/86 is below the 140/90 referral threshold.
Wrong - 37.4 °C is not a fever.
Wrong - this is a normal pattern for established labour.
Correct - a fetal heart rate below 110/min is an urgent referral criterion.
Wrong - 3 cm with intact membranes is normal latent or early labour.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old low-risk primigravida at term is being observed at a Klinik Kesihatan with a birthing centre. She has regular painful contractions, and the midwife is recording vital signs, fetal heart rate, contractions and pad checks on the Labour Progress Chart.
At what point should the partograph be commenced?
o: As soon as regular painful contractions begin
When the cervix is 2 cm dilated and effaced
When the cervix reaches 4 cm in active labour
Only after the membranes rupture spontaneously
At full dilatation, when active pushing begins
mcq.e: In early (latent) labour the **Labour Progress Chart** records maternal and fetal observations and pad checks. Once the woman is in **active labour, at a cervix of 4 cm or more**, the **partograph** is started so that progress can be plotted against the alert and action lines. Starting it in latent labour makes slow but normal latent labour look like failure to progress and leads to needless intervention.
w: Wrong - contractions alone may be latent labour, which is recorded on the Labour Progress Chart.
Wrong - 2 cm is still latent labour.
Correct - the partograph starts in active labour, from 4 cm.
Wrong - membrane status does not define when the partograph starts.
Wrong - by full dilatation the first-stage record would be missing.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old G3P2 at 40 weeks presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with regular contractions. Her membranes ruptured 1 hour ago and the liquor on the pad is thick and dark green. BP 122/76 mmHg, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 142/min, cervix 5 cm.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue monitoring at the clinic and reassess in 4 hours
Arrange urgent transfer to hospital with continued fetal monitoring
Start the partograph and plan delivery at the clinic
Send her home to return when contractions are 5 minutes apart
Start oral antibiotics and review progress in 2 hours
mcq.e: **Meconium-stained liquor** is an **urgent referral** criterion even when the fetal heart rate is normal at present, because it may signal fetal compromise and carries a risk of **meconium aspiration**. The baby needs continuous monitoring and a team ready for neonatal resuscitation in hospital. Stabilise, keep monitoring the fetal heart and transfer.
w: Wrong - meconium needs hospital-level monitoring now, not reassessment later.
Correct - meconium-stained liquor is an urgent referral criterion.
Wrong - a primary-care birthing centre is not equipped for this risk.
Wrong - she is in active labour with a high-risk sign.
Wrong - meconium is not an infection problem, and the delay is unsafe.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old G3P2 at 38 weeks is in labour at a Klinik Kesihatan. Her membranes rupture suddenly and the midwife sees a loop of umbilical cord at the introitus. The cervix is 6 cm and the fetal heart rate has dropped to 96/min. The ambulance has been called.
What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Lift the presenting part off the cord in the knee-chest position
Push the cord back into the uterus above the presenting part
Pull gently on the cord to check that it is still pulsating
Ask her to push hard to deliver the baby at the clinic
Lie her flat and wait for the fetal heart rate to recover
mcq.e: **Cord prolapse** is an urgent referral criterion and an obstetric emergency, because compression of the cord between the presenting part and the pelvis cuts off fetal oxygen. While transfer is arranged, **relieve compression**: manually elevate the presenting part, use the knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position (bladder filling may be used for longer transfers), and handle the cord as little as possible. Replacing or pulling the cord causes vasospasm, and a 6 cm cervix cannot deliver quickly in primary care.
w: Correct - elevating the presenting part and knee-chest positioning relieve cord compression.
Wrong - pushing the cord back causes vasospasm and is not recommended.
Wrong - handling and traction cause cord vasospasm.
Wrong - at 6 cm a vaginal birth is not imminent and pushing worsens compression.
Wrong - lying flat does not relieve compression and waiting allows hypoxia.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks walks into a Klinik Kesihatan with an alternative birthing centre in early labour. She had an emergency lower segment Caesarean section 2 years ago for fetal distress. BP 118/72 mmHg, fetal heart rate 138/min, cervix 3 cm, clear liquor. She would like to deliver at the clinic because she lives nearby.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Deliver at the birthing centre as she is low risk this pregnancy
Start an oxytocin infusion to shorten labour and reduce scar stress
Send her home and advise her to return when contractions are stronger
Monitor at the clinic and transfer only if labour stops progressing
Arrange transfer for delivery in hospital with continuous monitoring
mcq.e: A **previous Caesarean or uterine surgery** is an obstetric risk factor that rules out delivery in a primary-care birthing centre. A trial of labour after Caesarean carries a risk of **uterine rupture**, so it needs **hospital delivery** with continuous fetal monitoring and theatre on hand. Oxytocin raises the rupture risk further and is used only in hospital under specialist care.
w: Wrong - a uterine scar makes her high risk whatever this pregnancy has been like.
Wrong - oxytocin increases the risk of scar rupture and is not given in primary care.
Wrong - she is in labour with a scarred uterus and needs hospital care now.
Wrong - rupture can be sudden; waiting for poor progress is unsafe.
Correct - a previous Caesarean needs labour and delivery in hospital.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old G2P1 with a normal BP arrives at a Klinik Kesihatan fully dilated, and the midwife delivers a healthy baby within 10 minutes. Abdominal palpation confirms there is no second baby. The placenta has not yet delivered and there is moderate fresh bleeding.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Strong fundal pressure to push the placenta out
Wait for the placenta to deliver before giving any uterotonic
Oxytocin 10 units IM, then controlled cord traction
Misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally as first-line
Ergometrine 0.5 mg IV as a rapid bolus
mcq.e: **Active management of the third stage** is the main way to prevent **postpartum haemorrhage**: give **oxytocin 10 units IM** within a minute of birth once another baby has been excluded, then deliver the placenta by **controlled cord traction** with counter-pressure above the pubis, followed by uterine massage. Fundal pressure can cause uterine inversion, waiting increases blood loss, and IV ergometrine bolus causes severe hypertension and vomiting.
w: Wrong - fundal pressure risks uterine inversion and is not part of active management.
Wrong - physiological management increases blood loss; a uterotonic is given straight away.
Correct - IM oxytocin 10 units after excluding a twin, then controlled cord traction.
Wrong - misoprostol is a second-line option when oxytocin is unavailable.
Wrong - IV bolus ergometrine causes severe hypertension and is not first-line.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 7 minutes in a Klinik Kesihatan. He is on his side with oxygen, and capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. Two attempts at IV cannulation have failed.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Keep trying IV access until a line is in, then give IV diazepam
Give buccal or intranasal midazolam now
Give IM phenytoin into the anterolateral thigh
Give oral diazepam syrup through the side of the mouth
Wait until the seizure reaches 30 minutes before giving a drug
mcq.e: A seizure lasting **5 minutes or more** is treated as **status epilepticus**, and a benzodiazepine is given straight away. With **no IV access**, **buccal or intranasal midazolam** is first-line; rectal diazepam is an alternative. One repeat dose may be given if needed, and urgent transfer is arranged. Delaying treatment while chasing a line makes the seizure harder to stop, IM phenytoin is erratic and damages tissue, and nothing is put in a fitting patient’s mouth to swallow.
w: Wrong - repeated attempts delay treatment of a seizure that is already beyond 5 minutes.
Correct - buccal or intranasal midazolam is first-line when there is no IV access.
Wrong - IM phenytoin is erratically absorbed and causes tissue damage.
Wrong - oral drugs cannot be swallowed safely during a seizure and risk aspiration.
Wrong - treatment starts at 5 minutes; 30 minutes is the old definition.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on twice-daily premixed insulin is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan after his wife found him sweaty and jerking all four limbs. He is still fitting. Airway is supported, SpO2 96% on oxygen and an IV cannula is in place. Capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: IV diazepam 10 mg slowly
IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg infusion
IV magnesium sulphate 4 g slowly
IV 50% dextrose 50 mL
IV thiamine 100 mg alone
mcq.e: **Checking glucose** is a core step in every fitting patient, because **hypoglycaemia** is a reversible cause that anticonvulsants will not fix. This insulin-treated man has a glucose of 1.9 mmol/L, so **IV dextrose** corrects the cause and usually stops the seizure. Benzodiazepines are given if the fit continues after glucose is corrected. Thiamine is added before or with glucose in suspected alcohol misuse, but it never replaces glucose.
w: Wrong - a benzodiazepine does not correct the hypoglycaemia that is driving the seizure.
Wrong - phenytoin is second-line for status epilepticus and ignores the cause.
Wrong - magnesium is for eclampsia, not hypoglycaemic seizures.
Correct - IV dextrose corrects hypoglycaemia, the reversible cause of this seizure.
Wrong - thiamine alone leaves life-threatening hypoglycaemia untreated.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old man falls to the floor in the waiting area of a Klinik Kesihatan and starts a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. It began 1 minute ago. His brother grabs a metal spoon and shouts that he will bite off his tongue.
What should the staff nurse do first?
o: Move hard objects away, cushion his head and time the seizure
Put a padded spoon between his teeth to stop him biting his tongue
Hold his arms and legs down firmly to stop the jerking
Force his jaw open and pull his tongue forward
Splash cold water on his face to bring him round
mcq.e: During a seizure: **protect from injury, protect the airway, time the seizure, check ABC and glucose**. Do **not restrain**, do **not put anything in the mouth** and do **not force the mouth open**, because these cause broken teeth, aspiration and injury to the patient and the helper. Timing matters because a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus and needs a benzodiazepine. Once the jerking stops, place him in the recovery position.
w: Correct - protecting from injury and timing the seizure come first.
Wrong - objects in the mouth break teeth and can be inhaled.
Wrong - restraint causes fractures and dislocations and does not stop the seizure.
Wrong - forcing the jaw open causes injury; the tongue cannot be swallowed.
Wrong - water does not stop a seizure and may be aspirated.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old woman faints while standing in a long, hot queue at a Klinik Kesihatan. She first felt light-headed, nauseated and hot, and her vision went grey. A witness saw a few irregular jerks of her arms for about 10 seconds. She was fully alert within a minute, is pale and sweaty, with no tongue bite and no confusion. Capillary glucose is 5.4 mmol/L.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure
Focal impaired awareness seizure
Vasovagal syncope with brief jerks
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure
Hypoglycaemic seizure
mcq.e: **Not every fit is epilepsy.** A typical trigger (prolonged standing, heat), a prodrome of light-headedness, nausea and greying vision, **pallor and sweating**, a few brief jerks and **rapid recovery with no post-ictal confusion** mean **vasovagal syncope**; brief myoclonic jerks are common when the brain is briefly underperfused. A tonic-clonic seizure usually lasts longer, may cause tongue biting, and is followed by post-ictal confusion.
w: Wrong - tonic-clonic seizures are followed by post-ictal confusion, often with tongue biting.
Wrong - focal impaired awareness seizures have automatisms and post-ictal confusion, not a faint prodrome.
Correct - trigger, prodrome, pallor, brief jerks and immediate recovery mean syncope.
Wrong - PNES is usually longer, with eyes closed and fluctuating movements, and not a vasovagal prodrome.
Wrong - her glucose is normal.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home that lasted 2 minutes. She had headache and blurred vision since the morning and has no history of epilepsy. She is drowsy but breathing; BP 168/110 mmHg, urine protein 3+. An IV line is in place and transfer is being arranged.
Which drug should be given to prevent further seizures?
o: IV diazepam 10 mg as the definitive treatment
IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg as a loading infusion
IV labetalol alone to bring the BP down
Oral sodium valproate as a loading dose
IV magnesium sulphate 4 g as a loading dose
mcq.e: A seizure with **hypertension and proteinuria** after 20 weeks is **eclampsia**, and pregnancy is an **immediate referral** criterion for seizures. **Magnesium sulphate** (4 g IV loading dose given slowly, then maintenance) is the anticonvulsant of choice and prevents recurrence better than diazepam or phenytoin. BP must also be controlled, but an antihypertensive alone does not prevent fits; valproate is teratogenic and has no role.
w: Wrong - diazepam may stop a fit but is inferior to magnesium in preventing recurrence.
Wrong - phenytoin is less effective than magnesium in eclampsia.
Wrong - BP control is needed but does not prevent eclamptic seizures on its own.
Wrong - valproate is teratogenic and is not used for eclampsia.
Correct - magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice to prevent further eclamptic seizures.

mcq.stem:
A 4-month-old baby is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan after a generalised seizure lasting 2 minutes at home. He has had a fever of 38.6 °C since this morning. He is now feeding but sleepy, with a full anterior fontanelle. Capillary glucose is 5.0 mmol/L.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure the parents that this is a simple febrile seizure and give paracetamol
Refer immediately to hospital for evaluation, including for CNS infection
Prescribe rectal diazepam for home use and review in 1 week
Arrange an outpatient EEG and review the result in the clinic
Start oral amoxicillin and review in the clinic tomorrow
mcq.e: Febrile seizures occur between **6 months and 5 years**. A seizure with fever in an **infant under 6 months** is an **immediate referral** criterion because it often signals **meningitis or encephalitis**, which are hard to detect clinically at this age; a full fontanelle and drowsiness add to the concern. He needs hospital assessment including a septic work-up and lumbar puncture.
w: Wrong - febrile seizures are not diagnosed under 6 months; CNS infection must be excluded.
Correct - an infant under 6 months with a seizure needs immediate referral.
Wrong - home benzodiazepines do not address a possible CNS infection.
Wrong - an outpatient EEG delays urgent assessment for infection.
Wrong - oral antibiotics may partly treat and mask meningitis.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan by his wife after an episode at dinner. He said he had a strange rising feeling in his stomach and a sense of déjà vu, then stared blankly, smacked his lips and fumbled with his shirt buttons for about 90 seconds. He did not respond to her voice, did not fall, and was confused for 10 minutes afterwards with no memory of the event.
Which type of seizure is this?
o: Generalised absence seizure
Generalised tonic-clonic seizure
Focal aware seizure
Focal impaired awareness seizure
Generalised myoclonic seizure
mcq.e: An aura (rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu), then **unresponsiveness with automatisms** (lip smacking, fumbling) and **post-ictal confusion** is a **focal impaired awareness seizure**, typically of temporal lobe origin: it **starts in one area with impaired awareness**. Absence seizures last seconds, mainly affect children and leave no post-ictal confusion. In a focal aware seizure awareness is kept, and a generalised seizure involves both hemispheres from onset.
w: Wrong - absence seizures last seconds, have no aura and no post-ictal confusion.
Wrong - he did not stiffen, jerk or fall.
Wrong - he lost awareness and could not respond, so awareness was impaired.
Correct - aura, automatisms, unresponsiveness and post-ictal confusion mean a focal impaired awareness seizure.
Wrong - myoclonic seizures are brief shock-like jerks with awareness usually kept.
